t.su nuraxi di barumini@39.7,9.0:
Nobody quite knew what lay under the mound outside Barumini until the 1950s, when the archaeologist Giovanni Lilliu, himself a native of the village, began to dig. What emerged was the most complete nuragic complex on Sardinia: a central stone tower built in the Bronze Age, later surrounded by a bastion with four corner towers and an outer wall, and beyond that the remains of a village of round huts. Su Nuraxi was added to the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1997, and it remains the best place on the island to understand the nuragic civilisation, which left thousands of these towers across Sardinia.

Visits are guided and take you through the narrow passageways, up stairs inside the thick walls and into the chambers of the towers. The stones are massive, laid without mortar, and the engineering is remarkable. The village huts, with their stone benches and hearths, give a sense of daily life. Across the road, Casa Zapata, the former residence of a Spanish noble family, has been turned into a museum built over another nuraghe discovered beneath it.

Barumini lies in the Marmilla, a region of gentle, rounded hills, wheat fields and small villages in south-central Sardinia. Just to the north rises the Giara di Gesturi, a basalt plateau covered with cork oaks and seasonal ponds, home to a population of small wild horses found nowhere else in Europe. Seeing them grazing among the trees, especially in spring, is a delight.

The riding is relaxed and scenic. The roads through the Marmilla roll gently over the hills, with long views and little traffic. The road up to the Giara is narrower and winding, with a few hairpins and rough patches. Further east, the roads climb into the mountains of the Sarcidano and the Barbagia, where the riding becomes more challenging and spectacular.

Barumini is small, with a few bars and a restaurant or two, but fuel is more reliable in larger towns such as Sanluri or Villamar. In summer, the heat in the Marmilla can be intense, and there is little shade at the site, so visit early in the morning or late in the afternoon. Bring water and a hat, and allow at least an hour for the visit. Afterwards, find a bar in the village and sit for a while with a cold drink and a plate of local cheese.
t.viking age ring fortresses@57.0,9.3:
Around the year 980, King Harald Bluetooth of Denmark, the man who claimed on the great Jelling stone to have made the Danes Christian, built a series of perfectly circular fortresses across his kingdom, with ramparts laid out in precise geometric plans, gates at the four points of the compass and long houses arranged in squares inside. Aggersborg, on the northern shore of the Limfjord near Løgstør, was the largest of them, with a diameter of some two hundred and forty metres, and it is one of the Viking-Age Ring Fortresses listed by UNESCO in 2023, along with Fyrkat, Trelleborg, Nonnebakken and Borgring.

The fortresses were used for only a short time, and their purpose is still debated: perhaps they were military bases, perhaps centres of royal power, perhaps a way of controlling the kingdom during a time of unrest. At Aggersborg, the rampart has been partly reconstructed, and the outline of the fortress, with its gates and streets, is marked in the grass. A visitor centre explains the history. Standing on the rampart, looking out over the fjord, you can imagine the ships that once sailed past.

The Limfjord is a long, winding sound that cuts across northern Jutland from the North Sea to the Kattegat, with islands, bays and inlets, and the landscape around it is gently rolling, with fields, heaths and small towns. The light here is soft and clear, and the sky enormous. The wind is a constant companion, often strong, especially in autumn and winter.

For riders, northern Jutland offers relaxed riding on quiet roads through farmland, along the fjord and to the coast. The roads are generally good, with gentle curves and little traffic, but the landscape is flat, and the wind can make riding tiring. To the west, the North Sea coast, with its dunes, beaches and fishing villages, is wild and beautiful. Ferries cross the Limfjord at several points, small boats that add charm to any route.

Løgstør, a small town about four kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants, and its harbour and the Frederik VII canal, built in the nineteenth century to bypass the shallows of the fjord, are worth a look. The Limfjord is famous for its mussels and oysters, and a plate of fresh mussels steamed in white wine, with bread and a glass of beer, makes a fine meal. Aars, a larger town, is about twenty-six kilometres away.
t.knudeklint@56.8,9.0:
Fur is a small island in the Limfjord in northern Jutland, reached by a short ferry crossing, and on its northern coast, the cliffs of Knudeklint show one of the most remarkable geological sections in Denmark. The cliffs are made of moler, a light, porous clay formed from the skeletons of countless tiny algae, diatoms, that settled on the bottom of a sea some fifty-five million years ago. Through the pale moler run dark bands of volcanic ash, around a hundred and eighty of them, from eruptions in the North Atlantic as the ocean opened between Greenland and Europe. The layers have been folded and tilted by the glaciers of the ice age, creating dramatic patterns in the cliff face.

The moler of Fur is also rich in fossils: fish, insects, birds, turtles and plants, preserved in extraordinary detail, sometimes with soft tissues intact. The Fur Museum, on the island, displays many of these finds, and you may find fossils yourself on the beach below the cliffs, though digging in the cliffs is not allowed. Fur is part of a geological area that Denmark has worked to have recognised internationally, and the cliffs are protected.

The island is small, about twenty square kilometres, with farmland, heath, small villages and a quiet, peaceful atmosphere. The views from the hills, across the fjord to the neighbouring islands and the mainland, are lovely. The ferry from Branden on the mainland takes only a few minutes and runs frequently.

For riders, Fur and the surrounding area offer gentle, relaxed riding on quiet roads through farmland and along the fjord, with the island of Mors to the west, home of the cliffs of Hanklit, which also show the moler, and the Salling peninsula to the east. The roads are narrow and generally good, and traffic is light, but the wind can be strong, and the landscape is mostly flat. Ferries and bridges link the islands and peninsulas of the Limfjord, making for interesting routes.

Facilities on Fur are limited to a few shops, a museum, a brewery and some restaurants and accommodation; for fuel and more services, Nykøbing Mors, about eight kilometres away across the water, and Skive, on the mainland, are larger. Try a plate of fresh fish or mussels from the fjord, and a glass of beer from the island's brewery. And walk along the beach below Knudeklint, looking at the layers of ash in the cliff, a record of volcanic eruptions far away and long ago.
t.fyrkat@56.6,9.8:
Around the year 980, Harald Bluetooth, king of the Danes, built a ring of fortresses across his kingdom, and Fyrkat is the best-preserved of them. It is a perfect circle of earth and timber rampart about 120 metres across, with four gates at the compass points and streets crossing in the middle, and inside the ring, sixteen longhouses arranged in groups of four around a square. Tree-ring dating of the timbers points to the early 980s, and the neat plan and the way it echoes the other ring forts at Trelleborg and Aggersborg suggest a single royal design. Why the forts were built is still argued over, though they probably combined military, administrative and royal power at a time when Harald was uniting Denmark and bringing in Christianity.

The site lies on a hill above the Onsild river just outside Hobro, a town of about 11,000 people at the head of the Mariager Fjord. A reconstructed longhouse stands inside the ring, and the museum shows finds from the dig, among them the grave of a woman who may have been a seeress, buried with a staff and seeds of henbane. The ramparts are low now and covered in grass, and the best way to understand the plan is to walk the circle and follow the lines of the houses marked in the turf.

Getting here is easy. The roads of eastern Jutland are gentle, with rolling fields, hedged lanes and beech woods, and the speed limits are strictly enforced by cameras. Wind can be strong near the coast, and showers pass quickly, so take a light waterproof. To the south lie the Rold Skov forest and the hills at Rebild, which are among the most pleasant places to ride in the region, with bends that rise and fall through heather and trees.

Hobro has fuel stations, supermarkets and cafés, and the harbour on the fjord is a good place for a coffee. The nearby town of Mariager, with its cobbled lanes and roses on the cottage walls, is worth a detour. Try a smørrebrød or a hot dog from a roadside kiosk, a Danish institution. Spring and early summer, with long light evenings, are good times to visit, and the site is quiet on weekdays.
t.aggersborg@57.0,9.3:
Aggersborg is the giant of the Danish ring forts, and it is hard to appreciate until you see how much of it you cannot see. The circle, about 240 metres across, was twice the width of Fyrkat, with twelve gates, a rampart of earth and timber, and about forty-eight longhouses inside, set out in the same regular pattern of four-house groups. It was built around 980, in the reign of Harald Bluetooth, on a high bank above the Limfjord at one of its narrowest crossings, and it is thought to have controlled the water route through northern Jutland. A medieval church now stands on the site, and a section of the rampart is visible, along with markers showing where the gates and houses were.

The setting is wide and open. The Limfjord is a long, shallow, brackish waterway that cuts across northern Jutland and has made the area an island in all but name, and the fortress stood on its southern bank, facing the water. From the rampart you look north across the fjord to flat fields, with a ferry route nearby and the sky wide overhead. A small museum, the Aggersborg Viking Centre, helps explain the plan and the finds.

For a rider, northern Jutland is a place of space and wind. The roads are straight and flat, with long views across the fields to the fjord, and the weather changes quickly. A westerly can be strong, and showers cross the sky, with bright light between them. Traffic is light, and the main limit is the wind. The ferry across the fjord is a pleasant way to cross, and the small roads on either side are quiet. The best months are May to September.

The nearest small towns are Løgstør, with about 4,500 people on the fjord, and Fjerritslev and Brovst farther to the west, and for a larger place with a good supermarket you would use Aars, about 26 km away. Løgstør is known for its harbour and its old canning industry, and the fjord produces mussels and oysters. A plate of fish and chips or fried plaice at the harbour is a simple and good lunch. If you are following the Viking theme, this is the biggest fortress of the lot, and it is humbling to see how much work went into it.
t.jelling mounds@55.8,9.4:
Denmark's most important field is Jelling, which has two large grass mounds, a medieval church standing between them, and two carved runestones that count among the most important monuments of the country. The stones were raised in the tenth century. The smaller one was made by King Gorm the Old in memory of his wife Thyra, and the larger, with a crucified Christ on one face, was made by his son Harald Bluetooth, who boasted that he had won all of Denmark and Norway and made the Danes Christian. That is why it is often called the birth certificate of the nation. Harald's nickname, incidentally, is where the Bluetooth wireless logo comes from, a bind-rune of his initials.

The setting is gentle, rolling green country in the middle of Jutland, not far from the head of the Vejle Fjord. The church is white and small, and the mounds are big enough to make you look twice. There is a modern visitor centre next to the site, which does a good job of explaining the Viking royal seat, so allow an hour even if you are only on the ride for the scenery.

The riding around Jelling is some of the easiest in Europe. Roads are well kept, quiet and mostly gently winding, with long views over fields and the occasional wooded valley. There are few really challenging bends, but the scenery is soft and green, and early summer evenings are lovely. Speed limits are enforced firmly here, with cameras and a police presence on the main roads, so treat the limits seriously.

Jelling has about three thousand people, enough for fuel and food, and Vejle, nine kilometres east, is a proper town of over fifty thousand with everything you might need. The famous Hærvejen, the old Army Road, runs not far away, and reminds you that this was an ancient crossing of the peninsula long before the kings arrived. It is a dignified, slightly understated place that gets better the longer you look.
t.necropolis of montessu@39.1,8.7:
The Sulcis, in the south-west of Sardinia, is a landscape of cork oaks, bare hills and old mines, and Montessu lies in a quiet corner of it. The necropolis here is a cliff of pale trachyte rock, pierced by dozens of small chambers cut out by hand more than five thousand years ago. The Sardinians call such tombs domus de janas, houses of the fairies, and the name suits them: little rooms with doorways, ceilings and carved details like beams and, in a few, the spiral and horned symbols of a religion we only half understand. The site is managed locally, and opening arrangements vary, so check before you go.

The setting is part of the attraction. The rock stands in a valley of grass and scrub, with the sound of cowbells and crickets and the smell of wild herbs. The bare rock face shines in the late afternoon sun, and the doorways make dark squares in the stone. The tombs belong to the Ozieri culture, one of the great Neolithic cultures of the island, which also left behind the beautiful pottery and figurines now held in the museum at Cagliari.

The roads in the Sulcis are among the best in Sardinia for a rider. They climb through cork forest and over low passes, with tight bends, empty straights and long views to the sea. The surfaces are mostly good, with the odd patch of gravel, and traffic is very light. The coast road to the west, with its dunes and sea cliffs, is spectacular. Heat in summer is fierce, so start early. Wild boar and goats appear without warning, so keep an eye out, especially at dusk.

Villaperuccio, the nearest village, has just over nine hundred people, and Narcao a few more. Carbonia, with twenty-one thousand, was founded as a mining town in 1938 and is the place to find fuel, shops and rooms. Santadi, to the south, makes good wine from the Carignano grape.

Come in spring or autumn. The island is warm and green, and the roads are at their best. The Su Nuraxi at Barumini, on this ride, is a very different monument from the Bronze Age, an impressive nuragic fortress farther north.
t.cagliari@39.2,9.1:
Cagliari is a port city that grew on hills, and that is the key to understanding it. The capital of Sardinia climbs from the harbour up a steep rock crowned by Castello, the old walled quarter, which the Pisans fortified in the thirteenth century with two white limestone towers that still stand, the Torre dell'Elefante and the Torre di San Pancrazio. From the ramparts you can look across the whole gulf, the salt pans, the long white beach of Poetto and the low mountains beyond. The city's history is as layered as its streets. Phoenicians founded a port here, the Romans built an amphitheatre cut into the rock, and Aragonese and Spanish rulers added churches and palaces.

Nature is close at hand. The Molentargius salt pans, on the edge of the city, are a shallow wetland where flocks of pink flamingos feed, and they are visible from the road, which is a surprise in a city of this size. Poetto beach, about eight kilometres long, is the city's backyard, crowded in summer and almost empty in winter. Seafood dominates the menu, with bottarga, the cured fish roe, and fregola, tiny toasted pasta, appearing often. In the market of San Benedetto, one of the largest covered markets in Italy, fish, cheese and vegetables are piled high.

For a rider, Cagliari is a good base for exploring the south of the island. The state road to the north, known as the Carlo Felice, runs the length of Sardinia, and one early detour leads to Su Nuraxi at Barumini, about sixty kilometres north, a Bronze Age stone fortress that is a UNESCO site. The nuraghi, conical stone towers built by Sardinia's ancient civilisation over three thousand years ago, are scattered all over the island, and nobody knows exactly what they were for. Roads on the island are generally in good condition, with long curves and fine views, and traffic is light outside the cities. Summer is hot, with the best riding in spring and autumn.

Fuel and workshops are easy to find, and parking in the old centre is difficult, so leave the bike outside the old town gates. Evening is the time for aperitivo on the terraces, when the city lights come on across the bay.
t.bell gorge@-17.0,125.3:
Bell Gorge is one of the best-known swimming holes of the Kimberley, a series of falls tumbling over red sandstone into a deep green pool in the King Leopold Ranges in the north of Western Australia. It sits well off the Gibb River Road, reached by a rough track of around thirty kilometres from the main road to the Silent Grove campground, and then a walk of about a kilometre or so over rocks to the top of the falls. The dry season, roughly May to October, is the only time you can sensibly get here; in the wet, the road is cut by floods and closed.

The Gibb River Road itself runs about 660 kilometres from Derby to Kununurra and was first built to move cattle from the stations to the coast. Most of it is unsealed. Expect gravel with corrugations that can shake loose a loosely packed bike, patches of bulldust, rocky creek crossings and stretches of rough surface that deserve respect. Many riders on heavy touring bikes find it hard going, and lighter dual-sports cope better. Carry water, tools, spare tubes and a way to call for help, because phone coverage is almost nil, and passing traffic can be hours apart.

The land belongs to Aboriginal peoples, including the Bunuba, Wunambal and Ngarinyin, whose rock art with the Wandjina figures is found throughout this part of the Kimberley, and some sites are not open to casual visitors. Respect signage and fees. Around the gorge the country is savanna woodland with boab trees, spinifex on the stony slopes and pandanus along the creek lines. Freshwater crocodiles live in the Kimberley's pools, and the local ranger information tells you where swimming is safe.

Fuel is the deciding factor. Supplies are available at only a few roadhouses and stores along the Gibb River Road, such as Imintji and Mount Barnett, and a prudent rider carries extra and confirms availability before leaving Derby or Kununurra. Heat is intense by midday, so start early, and keep cool in the pool afterwards.
t.mount barnett@-16.7,126.0:
Mount Barnett is a cattle station in the middle of the Gibb River Road, and a roadhouse that every rider on that road ends up in, whether by plan or by thirst. It sits roughly halfway along the Kimberley's famous 660-kilometre track between Derby and Kununurra, and the Aboriginal-managed station runs the store, the campground and the fuel pumps that let you carry on in either direction.

The reason people stop is mostly practical. This is one of the few places along the road with fuel and cold drinks, and the shop sells basic supplies, ice and a meal, and is also where you pay camping and access fees for the nearby gorges. Manning Gorge is the big draw, with a campground a short ride off the main road and a walk of about an hour from there to a series of deep waterholes and a waterfall. The route involves crossing a wide pool, and walkers often float their packs over on air mattresses; riders should take that into account before they plan to carry cameras or valuables. Bring sturdy shoes and a hat, because the sun is fierce.

The road itself is the character of the place. The surface is mostly gravel and red dirt here, corrugated in places and graded by the shire at the start of each dry season, so conditions vary a lot from year to year and from week to week. After rain, even a short one, it becomes slick and dangerous. The Kimberley's wet season, from about November to April, closes sections of the route, and travel is sensible only from roughly May to October. Dust follows every vehicle, so keep a good gap from trucks and caravans.

Around the roadhouse the country is red earth, boab trees, and grey rocky hills, with the Barnett River winding between pools, and birdlife: kites, cockatoos, and in the evenings the croak of frogs. Dingoes sometimes slink around the campground. Be honest about your supplies: carry water, spare fuel if you can, and tell someone your plans. Prices here reflect how far everything has been trucked, so a cold drink comes dear, and nobody minds that you take your time.
t.windjana gorge@-17.4,125.0:
Windjana Gorge is where the Lennard River slices through the Napier Range in the west Kimberley, and the gorge walls are the remains of a Devonian reef, built by algae and corals when this country lay under a warm sea about 350 million years ago. Walking beside those cliffs you can see fossils in the limestone, shells and marine creatures, and the sheer scale of the place is humbling. The walls rise some thirty metres or more above a sandy river bed, which in the dry season shrinks to a chain of green pools.

Those pools are crowded with freshwater crocodiles, small and shy compared with their saltwater cousins, and they bask on the sand banks in surprising numbers. Do not swim, and keep a respectful distance from the edge. The place is also a breeding ground for thousands of fruit bats and corellas, and in the evening the sky fills with wings. The gorge is on Bunuba country, and the story of Jandamarra, a young Bunuba man who led a resistance against the pastoralists and police in the 1890s, is tied to this landscape. He was killed in 1897, near Tunnel Creek, and the story is still told with great respect.

The ride to the gorge is on gravel for the last part, so you need a bike that can handle corrugations, loose stones and the odd creek crossing, as well as good tyres and a plan. This part of the Gibb River Road is only passable in the dry season, roughly from May to October, and the wet season closes it altogether. Heat is intense, so start early, carry far more water than you think you need and tell someone your route.

Fuel is not available at the gorge. Plan to fill up at Derby or Fitzroy Crossing, and carry extra if your range is short, because distances here are long and help is far away. Camping at the gorge is simple, with basic facilities, and the night sky is superb. Nearby Tunnel Creek, a cave you can wade through with a torch, makes a good companion visit if time allows.
t.dougga thugga@36.4,9.2:
Dougga is the best-preserved Roman town in North Africa, and the Romans themselves would have understood why: the site sits on a hillside in the green farmland of northern Tunisia, looking over wheat country to a long ridge of low mountains. The modern town of Tabursuq lies a few kilometres away and has the fuel, bakeries and cafes. Allow a morning, and ideally arrive before the tour buses do.

The ride here is easy and pleasant, through olive groves, cereal fields and cork oak. Roads are narrow and the surface is variable, with potholes and occasional sand, and you share the lane with donkeys, scooters, shared taxis and flocks of sheep. In spring the hills are bright green and covered in wildflowers, while by late summer they have turned the colour of toast. Mid-afternoon in July is not the time to be on a black jacket, so leave early and carry plenty of water.

The history is the reason to come. Thugga began as a Numidian and Punic settlement, and a mausoleum from the second century BC still stands, one of the finest monuments of its kind, built for a Numidian chief and carrying inscriptions in the Libyan and Punic scripts. The Romans added a theatre that is astonishingly intact, a capitol with tall columns facing the plain, baths with elaborate under-floor heating and a temple of Saturn. Wealthy local families paid for much of it, which says something about how prosperous this grain-growing region was.

Tabursuq is the sensible place to buy fuel, and also to eat: grilled meat, bread and salads, mint tea, nothing grand. The site charges an entry fee, and guides will approach you. Take your time on the stone paths, which are uneven, and look at the view as well as the ruins. From the theatre you can imagine the audience seeing the same fields, only fewer of them in view. It is a quiet, unhurried place, and much more satisfying than a rushed visit.
t.changchuan tomb no 1@41.3,126.3:
Changchuan Tomb No. 1 is among the painted tombs of the ancient Koguryo kingdom, a state that ruled northern Korea and much of Manchuria from the first centuries BC until 668. The tomb itself lies on the Chinese bank, in a valley of fields and low hills where the Koguryo kings had one of their capitals.

What makes the Koguryo tombs remarkable is their art. The walls of the stone chambers were plastered and painted with scenes of daily life and spirit worlds, hunters on horseback, dancers, musicians, wrestlers, and the four guardian animals of the directions: the azure dragon, the white tiger, the red bird and the black tortoise-snake. The paintings, made between the fourth and seventh centuries, are among the earliest large surviving paintings in East Asia, and UNESCO included the tombs in 2004 as part of the capital cities and tombs of the ancient Koguryo kingdom.

Near Ji'an, the giant stepped pyramid known as the General's Tomb and the huge stele of King Gwanggaeto, a stone covered in carved characters that records his conquests, give a sense of the scale of the dynasty. The river is wide and green here, with mist in the morning, and the contrast between the two banks, one busy with new construction and one quiet and farmed, is striking. Autumn brings gold to the hillsides and winters are cold and dry.

This is a sensitive border area, so be realistic: access to the tomb interior is restricted to protect the paintings, and visitors should check what is open and follow local rules. Roads in the area are good and mostly quiet, and Ji'an has fuel, hotels and restaurants serving Korean-style dishes with a Chinese accent. Foreign riders will also need to think about permits and regulations for motorcycles in China, which are strict. Plan well, and the history is worth the effort.
t.holbrook@34.9,-110.2:
Holbrook is a small town on Interstate 40 in northern Arizona, a place that still looks like the postcard for old Route 66. About five thousand people live here, among sunbaked streets, neon signs and dusty sidewalks. The Wigwam Motel, a ring of concrete teepees with vintage cars parked outside, opened in the 1950s and is a favourite photo stop. Across the street, curio shops sell turquoise jewellery and rubber tomahawks, and the diners offer big breakfasts and tall milkshakes.

The town grew with the railroad in the 1880s and became a lawless cattle town, with a reputation for gunfights and the notorious Hashknife outfit, a vast ranch whose cowboys left plenty of stories. Today it is the county seat of Navajo County and a gateway to the Petrified Forest National Park, about twenty miles east, where logs of ancient stone, turned to quartz and agate, lie scattered across the Painted Desert's banded hills. The landscape is wide, empty and glowing, with layered colours of rose, grey and lavender in the evening light.

For a rider on Route 66, Holbrook is a prime stop. The old road survives in sections, parallel to the interstate, and it carries nostalgic traffic and a lot of European tourists on rented Harleys. The riding here is mostly straight and flat, with long views, big skies and strong crosswinds. Summer heat is intense, so start early and drink water, and thunderstorms in July and August can bring flash floods across low points. Winter is cold, with the occasional snowfall at this altitude of about a thousand five hundred metres.

Fuel is easy in town, and so are motels. Eat something local, perhaps Navajo tacos or a steak, and then walk the main street at sundown, when the neon flickers on and the heat eases. The Little Colorado River, normally dry, runs sandy and red through the landscape. Go early to the Petrified Forest to see the light on the rocks, and keep an eye out for pronghorn on the open range. It is a place that rewards slowing down.
t.yakutsk@62.0,129.7:
Yakutsk is the largest city in the world built on continuous permafrost, and it shows. Buildings stand on concrete piles driven into the frozen ground, so that the heat of the house does not melt what holds it up, and pipes run above ground in insulated boxes, since burying them is impossible. Winter here is among the coldest on Earth for a major city, with temperatures regularly below minus forty, and the air turns to a sparkling fog of ice crystals. Summer, by contrast, can be hot and bright, and the city sits on the great Lena River, a kilometre or more wide.

The Sakha people, also called Yakuts, are Turkic-speaking horse herders who migrated here centuries ago, and their culture is strong, with a rich epic tradition and a small hardy horse bred to survive the cold. Local food includes stroganina, thin shavings of frozen raw fish, eaten with salt and pepper, and horse meat. A museum in the city displays mammoth remains found in the thawing ground, and the permafrost institute has a tunnel in the frozen earth that you can visit.

The roads from here are legendary. The Kolyma Highway, known as the Road of Bones, was built by Gulag prisoners in the 1930s and 1940s, and thousands died along it. The start is across the Lena from Yakutsk at Nizhny Bestyakh, reached by a ferry in summer and an ice road in winter, and from there the road runs toward Khandyga and beyond, a route of gravel, mud and dust through endless forest. The Lena Highway south toward Neryungri is better, though still demanding. Distances are huge, services are rare, mosquitoes in July are fierce, and weather can change fast.

Yakutsk has more than two hundred thousand people, with fuel, food, hotels and repair shops. Fill up completely before leaving, carry spare fuel, tools and water, and tell someone your plans. Foreign riders should check current conditions and rules before planning travel.
t.el questro@-16.0,128.0:
El Questro began as a cattle station and became something else. This vast property in the East Kimberley, a short drive from the Gibb River Road's eastern end, was once a working pastoral lease, and it has been turned into a wilderness park, with gorges, hot springs and waterfalls set in a country of red cliffs and baobab trees. Emma Gorge, with its cool swimming hole beneath a high waterfall, and Zebedee Springs, a series of warm pools among palms, are the best known, and the walk into El Questro Gorge ends at a deep pool shaded by rock walls.

The Gibb River Road itself is a legend of Australian outback travel. It runs some six hundred and sixty kilometres through the Kimberley, originally built in the 1960s to carry cattle to the coast, and most of it is unsealed, corrugated gravel, with creek crossings and a few rough sections. The usual season is the dry, from about May to September, and in the wet, from roughly November to March, the road is closed by flooding. Ask for current conditions at a roadhouse or the visitor centre in Kununurra, about a hundred kilometres east, before heading in.

The turn-off to El Questro is marked by the Pentecost River crossing, a broad, shallow ford below the dramatic ridge of the Cockburn Range. It is a famous photograph spot and an obvious place to take care, since the crossing can be deep after rain, and crocodiles live in the Kimberley rivers. Never swim in a river or waterhole unless a local or a sign says it is safe, and be careful of the edge.

The riding is a serious undertaking. Corrugations shake loose bolts and can unsettle a bike, so ride a light, well-prepared machine with good tyres and a spare tube, carry plenty of water and tell someone your route. Dust is everywhere, and heat can be fierce, with afternoon temperatures well above thirty-five degrees even in the dry season.

Permafrost lies beneath the forest floor, the larches grow thin and straight, and in winter the river freezes into a highway for lorries. Summer is short and intense, with long days and a lot of insects, so bring repellent and a head net.

A boat trip along the river reveals the cliffs at their best, with the light changing from white to gold as the day goes on. If you are lucky you may see a Yakutian horse, a small, tough breed that grazes outdoors through winters of minus fifty. Take warm clothing even in July, because the wind on the water is cold, and keep your camera ready for the moment the pillars appear around a bend. They are a landscape that makes you feel very small, and very glad to have come.
t.archaeological park of pranu mutteddu@39:
The south of Sardinia is not all beaches. Inland, on the edge of the Gerrei hills, lies Pranu Mutteddu, a flat upland of granite, cork oak and scrub that holds one of the island's more striking prehistoric sites. The name means something like the plain of the little stones in Sardinian, and the place is known for its menhirs, standing stones raised several thousand years ago by Neolithic people, many of them still upright and arranged in rows or groups across the clearing.

The stones are a puzzle. There are dozens of them, some a couple of metres tall, and archaeologists believe they were bound up with burial and ritual, since the site also holds a number of small stone tombs and what look like funerary chambers. The people who built them left no writing, so what we have is shape and position: lines of grey slabs under the open sky, a great deal of space, and silence broken only by cicadas and the occasional tractor in the distance.

The ride in is part of the experience. The roads in this part of Sardinia leave the main highways behind and wind through the Flumendosa valley, with tight bends, hairpins on the climbs and the odd stretch of broken asphalt where the mountain has slumped onto the road. Traffic is almost non-existent, which is both a pleasure and a reason to be careful, because a mechanical problem will not have many witnesses. The Mulargia lake is not far off, and the road towards Villasalto and the Sarrabus mountains gives quiet, shaded riding among eucalyptus and holm oak.

Goni and Silius are very small villages, and fuel is not something to count on in either. Dolianova, about twenty-three kilometres off, is the nearest town with a proper range of services, and it is worth filling the tank there before you head into the hills. Take water with you in summer, because the plain has little shade and the sun is fierce from June to September. Spring is the best time, when the grass is green and wildflowers spread across the ground between the stones.
t.hanklit@56.9,8.8:
Hanklit is a cliff on the island of Mors, in the Limfjord, the broad, shallow fjord that cuts across northern Denmark and turns Jutland into an island. The cliff is made of moler, a grey-white clay full of diatoms, the tiny silica shells of ancient algae, laid down on the seabed some fifty-five million years ago, and the layers are interleaved with bands of black volcanic ash from eruptions in what is now the North Sea region. The folding of the strata, which were pushed and twisted by glaciers during the Ice Age, makes the cliff look like a layered cake that has been dragged sideways. Fossils of fish, insects, plants and birds are found in the moler, and it is quarried for insulating bricks and cat litter.

The Danish rides listed here are built around Fyrkat, the Viking ring fortress near Hobro, but Hanklit gives a different view of the north. The cliff rises abruptly from the shore of the fjord, with a path that climbs to a heath at the top, where heather, juniper and bird's-foot trefoil grow, and views over the water and the low green hills of Thy and Salling. Skylarks sing over the heath in spring. Seals sometimes rest on the shoals, and the wind is constant.

The riding on Mors and the surrounding Limfjord country is gentle and open, with small roads that go from farm to farm, past windmills and little churches. The land is flat or gently rolling, the surfaces are smooth, and the traffic is light. The sea breeze can be strong and cold, even in July, and showers come and go quickly, so a windproof jacket is wise. Danish speed rules are strict and controlled with cameras, and local drivers tend to follow them. Early summer, with its long evenings, is the best time, and in late June the light lingers until close to midnight.

Thisted, seven kilometres off across the fjord, is a town of thirteen thousand with fuel, supermarkets, a brewery and a handful of restaurants, and it is also a surfing hub, since the North Sea coast at Klitmøller attracts windsurfers and wave riders. On Mors, the village of Nykøbing has more services. Try a plate of smoked fish, a Danish hot dog from a kiosk, or a pastry in a bakery, and the local Thy beer. The path up Hanklit can be wet and slippery after rain, so wear shoes with grip, and keep clear of the unstable edge of the cliff.
t.ichkeul national park@37.2,9.7:
Ichkeul is a lake that behaves like a lung. In winter it fills with fresh water from the rivers of northern Tunisia, and thousands upon thousands of ducks, geese and coots arrive from Europe, making it one of the great wintering grounds on the migration route between the continents. In summer the sea creeps in from Lake Bizerte through a channel, the water turns brackish, and the birds leave. That seesaw between fresh and salt is the heart of the place, and UNESCO listed the national park in 1980 for its importance to waterfowl. The Tunisian state's dams on the feeding rivers have put the balance under strain, which is a story the park authorities have been wrestling with for years.

Rising from the southern shore of the lake is Jebel Ichkeul, a limestone ridge that stands at around five hundred metres, with old olive and carob trees on its slopes and raptors turning overhead. Down at its foot there is a small information point for visitors. Water buffalo, brought long ago, graze the shallow edges, which is unexpected in North Africa.

The ride in is quiet and very Tunisian. From the road between Bizerte and Mateur you pass through farmland with olives, wheat and artichokes, and the roads are usually decent but narrow, with donkey carts, scooters and overloaded vans. Spring is superb, when everything is green and the flowers cover the slopes, while from midsummer onward the heat flattens everything. Winter is the time for the birds, but also for rain and mud on the tracks around the lake.

Mateur, Menzel Bourguiba and Bizerte all have fuel and cafes, so fill up before heading into the park, which has little in the way of services. Bring water, and ask at the entrance about walking the mountain track, as access and opening times can change.

Behind all this sits a larger story. This part of Tunisia was Carthaginian, then Roman, and the great ruins of Dougga lie a morning's ride away to the south. It would be a mistake to treat the lake as only a bird sanctuary.
t.the bony fish fossils of the western lim:
On the small, flat island of Mors in the Limfjord, the cliffs are not made of chalk or granite but of a pale grey-white clay, laid down in the sea about fifty-five million years ago. This is the moler, a deposit of diatom earth interleaved with hundreds of thin layers of volcanic ash, and it is one of the best places in the world to find fossils from the early Eocene. Fish, insects, birds and plants have been found here, beautifully preserved, including the bony fish that give the site its name.

The ash fell from volcanoes in the area that is now the North Sea, and it settled on a warm, shallow sea where life was abundant. The fossils are fine and detailed, and the layering makes it possible to count the ash falls, like pages in a book. The moler was also dug for industrial use, as an insulating and absorbent material, and old pits around Mors and the island of Fur are part of the story. Fossil collecting at the cliffs is regulated, so it is best to follow local rules and ask at the museum.

Mors is a quiet and green place. The roads run across low, rolling farmland, with small villages, windbreaks and long views over the fjord, and the surface is generally good. The corners are few, so it is a ride of space and sky rather than of bends, and wind is the main factor, especially on exposed coastal sections. The bridge to the island is a pleasure in itself, and a small ferry to the island of Fur is a short hop away.

Nykøbing Mors, about eight kilometres away, is the main town, with nearly ten thousand people, a good range of shops, fuel and restaurants. Thisted, a little further, is larger. Danish food here includes fresh fish, smørrebrød, and the local beer from Thisted, and the cafés are good for a coffee and a pastry.

The ride links these cliffs with the Viking-age ring fortresses, particularly Fyrkat, so you move from a deep past of fossils to a recent past of kings. The best months are late spring and early autumn, when the light is long and the crowds are small.
t.moravian church settlements@55.4,9.5:
Christiansfeld is a town designed on a drawing board, and it still looks like it. It was founded in 1773 by the Moravian Church, the Brethren, a Protestant community from Bohemia and Saxony that had its centre at Herrnhut, and it was laid out on a strict grid around a central square, with a church at its heart. The houses are built of yellow brick, with red tile roofs, and they stand in neat rows with a gentle uniformity that has survived two and a half centuries. In 2015 the town was added to the World Heritage list.

The Moravians lived communally, with separate houses for single men, single women and widows, and with a common cemetery known as God's Acre, where all graves are marked with identical flat stones, to show that everyone is equal in death. The cemetery is a quiet, green place, with lawns and lime trees, and a walk through it is a calm experience. The town was also a place of craft and trade, and the Moravians' reputation for fair dealing brought customers from across Denmark.

The best-known product is the Christiansfeld honey cake, a spiced, flat biscuit that is still made in the town's bakery and sold in a shop that retains an old-fashioned feel. It is the right kind of snack for a rider, as it keeps well in a tank bag, and the smell of baking is a good guide when you arrive.

As a place to ride, southern Jutland is gentle. Roads run through rolling farmland, past red-brick farms and small woods, with long views and easy bends, and the surface is excellent. The Little Belt, the strait between Jutland and Funen, lies to the east, and the Kolding fjord is nearby. Wind can be strong, and the weather changes quickly, but the open country has a peaceful character.

Christiansfeld has about two and a half thousand people, with a petrol station, a supermarket and a few cafés, and Kolding, a larger town a short ride north, has more choice. The ride pairs the town with Nonnebakken in Odense, a Viking-age ring fortress on the island of Funen. Park near the square and walk, because the grid is compact and the old streets are best seen on foot.
t.needles@34.8,-114.6:
Needles takes its name from the jagged pinnacles that rise above the Colorado River on the Arizona side, and it is one of the hottest places in the United States, where summer temperatures regularly climb above forty-five degrees. Behind the town, the Needles peaks stand in a jagged row, and to the east the river curves in blue loops through the brown desert.

The town grew up with the railway. The Santa Fe line reached the Colorado in the 1880s, and the old Harvey House, El Garcés, a Spanish Colonial building of 1908 beside the tracks, once served travellers as a hotel and restaurant. It has been restored in recent years and is a good place to start. Needles was also the town where the Joad family in The Grapes of Wrath crossed the river on their way to California, and John Steinbeck described the desert and the dread of the crossing. Snoopy's brother Spike, from the Peanuts comic strip, lives here, and the town has a small tribute to him.

For a rider, the old Route 66 here is a relic. Beyond the town, the road runs through the Mojave, with long straight stretches, empty horizons and dry washes, and the surface varies between smooth and rough. In summer, the heat is serious, with temperatures that can exceed the tolerance of both bikes and riders, so start before dawn, carry plenty of water and avoid the middle of the day. In winter and spring, the weather is mild and the desert blooms with flowers after rain. Side roads lead to old mining camps and the Colorado River, where boats and fishing are popular.

Fuel, food and rest are easy in town, with several petrol stations, diners and motels along the main street. Bullhead City, thirty-four kilometres away, has more, and the next services in California, along the road to Barstow, are well spaced, so fill the tank and carry water before heading west. Look for a classic diner serving burgers, shakes and pie.

The sunsets here are huge and red. Park near the river, watch the light fade on the Needles and listen to the freight trains rumbling through the dusk. It is the very picture of the American West.
t.tortilla flat@33.5,-111.4:
Tortilla Flat is a tiny settlement on the Apache Trail, in the Superstition Mountains east of Phoenix, with a population that can be counted in single figures and a reputation far larger. It began as a stagecoach stop on the road built in 1905 to carry materials to the construction site of Roosevelt Dam, and today it consists of a restaurant, a saloon, a general store and a gift shop, all in a cluster of wooden buildings with a western look. Inside the saloon, the walls are covered with dollar bills, thousands of them, signed and stapled up by visitors, and the bar stools are saddles.

The mountains around it are rough, volcanic and full of legend. The Superstitions are said to hold the Lost Dutchman's Gold Mine, a treasure supposedly hidden by a prospector named Jacob Waltz in the nineteenth century, and people have been searching for it, and sometimes dying in the attempt, for more than a century. The scenery is a vivid desert, with saguaro cactus on the slopes, jagged cliffs and canyons that glow orange and red at sunset. Spring wildflowers, after a wet winter, carpet the hills with yellow and purple.

The Apache Trail, Arizona State Route 88, is the road that matters. It leaves Apache Junction and climbs through twisting curves, past Canyon Lake, a deep blue reservoir in a red canyon, to Tortilla Flat, and the pavement is narrow with tight bends and steep drops. Beyond the village, the road turns to gravel for around thirty kilometres, with narrow shelves cut into cliffs, steep grades and a famous switchback section that is unnerving in a car and demanding on a motorcycle. Check conditions before going on, because the surface can be rough or washed out after rain, and it is not for the inexperienced.

The restaurant serves chilli, burgers and a prickly pear ice cream that is a house speciality, and the place is crowded on weekends, with bikers and tour buses competing for parking. Summer temperatures are dangerous, often above forty degrees, so go in the cooler months, from October to April. The evenings are cool and the stars are brilliant, and a pause on the terrace with a cold drink is the right way to end the climb.
t.hjelmeland@59.2,6.2:
Hjelmeland is a small town on the Ryfylke coast, on the north side of Boknafjorden, and it is a place where the roads and the ferries meet. Ryfylke is a region of long, narrow fjords, steep slopes and farms, and the landscape is a mix of green hillsides, grey rock and dark water. The town sits at the head of a sheltered bay, with a harbour full of small boats, a church, and a main street of low buildings. It is a working place more than a tourist one, and its life depends on farming, fish farming and the ferries that connect it to its neighbours.

The ferry connection is the point of the place. Several routes cross the fjords here, and a rider planning the ride around Ryfylke has to think about timetables. Check them before you set out, buy tickets on board or by app, and arrive in good time, since in summer, the queue can be long. The ferry crossing is also a pleasure in its own right, a quiet half hour on a ship, with the mountains around you and the water beneath. Some of the fjords here are deep and cold, and the cliffs rise straight from the water.

The roads in Ryfylke are narrow, winding and often steep, climbing over the headlands between the fjords and dropping again to the water. The surface is good, but the bends are tight, and the traffic is light, with tractors and lorries more likely than tourists. In wet weather, the slopes can be slippery, with leaves and gravel at the corners. Wind can be strong where the fjords open to the sea. Sheep roam the roadsides in summer.

The countryside has a long history of farming, and the old farms, sometimes with turf roofs or red-painted barns, are scattered along the shore. Apples and berries grow in sheltered spots, and in autumn the colours are rich. Hjelmeland has a pump, shops and cafés, and it is a sensible place to buy food and fill the tank before you go on. Jørpeland, a larger town, lies to the south-west, and has a wider choice of services. In the long summer evenings, a ride along the water at nine o'clock, in a golden light, is one of the best things the region offers.
t.lovrafjorden@59.4,6.3:
Lovrafjorden is a quiet arm of water in the Ryfylke region, on the road through the country north-east of Stavanger, and it has the character of many Norwegian fjords: steep walls of rock, a narrow channel of dark water, and farms perched on small ledges above the shore. The surface of the water is often so still that the mountains double themselves in it, and early in the morning, with a thread of mist on the water, the effect is quiet and complete. The fjord is not one of the famous ones, and that is part of its charm. You may have it almost to yourself.

The road follows the shore and then climbs over the shoulder of the hills, with bends that are narrow and tight, and views that open and close. The surface is generally good, and the traffic is light, so it is a comfortable ride for those who like to take their time. Small bridges cross the streams that tumble down the slopes, and in spring, when the snow melts, the waterfalls are at their best. Rain is common, and mist can fill the fjord within minutes. Take warm and waterproof clothes, because the temperature falls quickly in the shade.

The story of this country is one of hard, patient work. Farmers cleared the slopes, built terraces and walls, and brought hay down from the high pastures on their backs, and many of the farms are now abandoned or used as summer homes. Hydropower came in the twentieth century, and with it dams, tunnels and power lines, which changed the valleys and the economy. In Sauda, nearby, industry took over from farming, and the town grew around the smelters and the power stations.

Fuel is the thing to plan. Small settlements along the fjord have little, and Sauda, the nearest town with a population of a few thousand, has a pump and a supermarket. Etne, on the other side of the hills, is smaller. Start the day with a full tank, and carry a snack and a flask. The best times are early morning and late evening, when the light is low, the air is still, and the water holds the colour of the sky.
t.sauda@59.7,6.4:
Sauda sits at the head of the Saudafjord, in a deep valley surrounded by high mountains, and it is a town built on industry rather than tourism. Hydropower was the foundation: the rivers that fall from the mountains drove turbines, and the power in turn fed smelters, which gave work to thousands in the twentieth century. The town's history is also one of mining. At Allmannajuvet, a gorge a short way outside the town, zinc was mined in the early twentieth century, and today the remains of the mine have been turned into a museum, with a striking modern building designed by the Swiss architect Peter Zumthor, part of the Norwegian scenic route programme. It is a rare place where the story of work is told with such care.

The setting is dramatic. The mountains rise steeply around the town, and in winter the sun barely reaches the valley floor, a fact the people of Sauda know well. In summer, long days and green slopes make up for it. The area is also a ski resort, with slopes above the town and a long season, and the Saudafjellet makes the town busy in winter.

For a rider, the roads in and out of Sauda are some of the best in this part of the country. The road from the south climbs over the mountains in long bends, passes lakes and dams, and drops to the town. The surface is good and traffic is light. The road to the north, along the fjord, is narrower and slower. Rain and fog are common, and ice can form on the high sections in autumn and spring. Winter brings snow, and some roads may be closed, so check conditions before you go.

With around four thousand people, Sauda has everything a rider needs: fuel stations, supermarkets, cafés and restaurants, and a choice of places to stay. It is the best place for a proper meal and a rest on this route, and the fuel stop to count on before the empty stretches of the Ryfylke mountains. Try the local bakery for a morning bun and coffee. The town is quiet in the evening, and the sound of water from the river is a constant companion, a reminder of the force that built the place.
t.latefossen@59.9,6.6:
Låtefossen is two waterfalls that fall side by side from the same stream, joining at the bottom under an old stone arch bridge, and the road runs straight across it. It is one of the few places in Norway where you can ride directly through the spray of a major waterfall. The total drop is about 165 metres, and the water thunders down the rock face in two white ropes that merge and rush under the bridge. On a wet day you will be soaked in seconds, and in summer the spray is a gift on a hot afternoon. There is a car park on the roadside, and a few steps lead to the bridge, so the stop is easy.

The setting is wild. The waterfall comes from the Folgefonna glacier, and meltwater and rain feed it, so the flow is greatest in late spring and after storms. The valley is steep and wooded, with moss, birch and fern on the slopes, and on a clear day you can see the white edge of the ice at the top. The sound of the water is constant and loud, and fills the valley. A stone bridge was built here in the nineteenth century, long before the road was widened, and old photographs show travellers stopping, just as we do now.

The road itself is Rv13, which runs from Odda toward the Hardanger fjord and the plateau, and it is a pleasant ride. The surface is good, the bends are long and easy, and the scenery includes forest, rock and water at almost every turn. Traffic is steady in summer, and tourist buses stop at the falls, so the car park can be crowded around midday. Aim for the morning, and take care on the bridge, which can be slick. If you stop, park off the carriageway and watch for traffic as you walk.

Odda, about fourteen kilometres away, is the nearest large town. It has fuel, shops and restaurants, and a history of heavy industry, with a zinc smelter that closed some time ago. It is also the starting point for the walk to Trolltunga, a rock ledge over a lake that is among Norway's most famous hikes, a long day's walk that is only open in summer. Odda is a good place to eat, rest and buy supplies. Bring a waterproof, and keep your camera in a bag.
t.orrestranda@58.7,5.5:
Orrestranda is a long, pale beach on the Jæren coast, one of the few stretches of Norway where the land is flat enough for sand and the sea breaks in proper surf. The coast here is a different world from the fjord country to the north and east: low, open, windswept farmland, with stone walls, potato fields and sheep, and a sea that rolls in from the North Sea without any islands to blunt it. The dunes behind the beach are covered in marram grass, the sky is huge, and the air tastes of salt. In summer the beach fills with families, and in autumn and winter surfers in thick wetsuits ride the waves, a sight that surprises people who think of Norway as nothing but mountains.

The road along the coast is flat and fast, with long straights and gentle bends, and the surface is good. It is a very different kind of riding from the fjord roads, more about wind and space than climbing and cornering. A crosswind can be strong, and gusts catch riders on exposed stretches, so keep your hands firm on the bars. Traffic is moderate, with farm machinery and local cars, and cyclists are common. The area is a favourite with cyclists, who use the dedicated routes along the shore.

Jæren is also a good place to see how Norway has used its land. The stone walls are made from rocks cleared from the fields by generations of farmers, and they stretch for kilometres in every direction. Near Orre, an old church stands among the fields, and the area has traces of settlement going back thousands of years. The soil is rich enough for vegetables, and you will often see roadside stalls selling potatoes, carrots and strawberries in the season.

Bryne, about seven kilometres away, is the nearest town with a decent range of services, and it has fuel, shops and cafés. Nærbø is another option. On the beach, parking is free or cheap, and there is often a kiosk selling ice cream and coffee in summer. Bring a layer even on a warm day, since the sea breeze is cool. At the end of the day, watch the sun go down over the sea, the sky filling with orange light, and the surfers silhouetted against it.
t.kvassheim lighthouse@58.5,5.7:
Kvassheim Lighthouse stands on a low, rocky point on the Jæren coast, a white tower that has been guiding ships past a dangerous shore since the early twentieth century. This stretch of the North Sea has claimed many vessels over the years, and the coast has a long history of wrecks, with rocks just under the surface and storms that arrive without warning. The lighthouse was built to prevent that, and for decades it was staffed by keepers and their families, who lived in the cottages next to the tower. Today it is a visitor site, with a small museum and a café in the old buildings, usually open in the summer season.

The setting is wide and bare, and the sea fills the whole western horizon. A beach of pale sand lies nearby, backed by dunes, and the shore is strewn with rocks and seaweed. The wind blows steadily, and the light is clear and cold. In winter, storms drive big waves onto the rocks, and spray can reach the lighthouse itself, a spectacular sight if you are well wrapped up and a safe distance back. In summer, the sea is calmer and families fill the beach. Birdlife is rich, with waders, gulls and ducks on the shore, and in spring and autumn migrants stop here on the way north or south.

The ride to the lighthouse is easy. The road runs across flat farmland, with straight stretches and gentle curves, and a surface in good condition. Traffic is light, apart from the odd tractor. The wind is the thing to watch, especially on the exposed coast, where it can push a bike sideways, and in rain the roads can be slick with mud from the farm vehicles. Slow down at the junctions, since visibility can be limited by the hedges and walls.

The nearest villages, Vigrestad and Varhaug, have shops and basic services, and Egersund, the nearest town of any size, is about twenty kilometres south, with fuel, supermarkets and restaurants. Bring warm clothes whatever the season, as a bright day in town can be raw by the sea. The café, when open, serves coffee, waffles and simple meals, and it is a fine place to sit and watch the weather come in from the west. Take time to walk along the shore, and look for the shapes of old wrecks in the rocks.
t.egersund@58.5,6.0:
Egersund is a harbour town on the south-west coast of Norway, with about nine and a half thousand people, a working fishing fleet and a layout of streets and quays that is easy to like. The old centre is a grid of white wooden houses, mostly low and neat, along a main street named Strandgata, and the harbour is lined with boats, cranes and fish processing plants. The town grew rich on herring and later on a famous faience factory, which produced fine ceramics from the 1840s until the late twentieth century, and a museum in town shows examples. Egersund pottery is still collected and sold in antique shops.

The town sits at a natural gap in the coast, with an island, Eigerøy, sheltering the harbour. A lighthouse stands on the far side of the island, reached by a bridge, and the road out is a pleasant ride with open views and a sense of the sea. The island is a good place to walk, with paths along the shore and plenty of birds. The fishing industry is still the basis of the local economy, and you will see trawlers and supply vessels in the port, along with ferries and fishing boats.

The road to Egersund runs along the coast through Jæren, a flat and windswept country, and then through low hills and forest as it nears the town. It is easy riding, with long straight sections and gentle bends, though the wind can be strong. Traffic is light to moderate, and heavier in summer. The E39 passes close, and heavy lorries use it, so take care on the junctions. Rain is common, and the roads can be wet and slick.

Because it is a real working town, Egersund has everything you need: fuel stations, supermarkets, banks, repair shops and a good selection of cafés and restaurants. It is the largest place for a good distance in either direction, which makes it the sensible place to fill up, eat and rest before the next leg. The harbour is a pleasant place to sit with a coffee and watch the boats, and a few restaurants serve fresh fish at reasonable prices. Try the local fish soup. Hotels are available, and the town is quiet in the evening, with the harbour lights reflecting on the water.
t.forsand ferry@58.9,6.1:
Forsand is a small settlement at the mouth of the Lysefjord, and the ferry here is the way into one of Norway's most dramatic landscapes. The fjord is about forty kilometres long and cuts into the mountains in a narrow, straight channel, with walls that rise a kilometre in places. These walls were carved by glaciers in the last ice age, and the grey rock, ancient gneiss, is smooth and pale in the light. Nearby, the cliff of Preikestolen, the Pulpit Rock, juts out about six hundred metres above the water, and the hike to it is among the most popular in the country.

The ferry crossing is part of the ride, and it gives you a chance to sit still and look. Norwegian ferries are efficient and frequent, with timetables posted at the quay and payment by card or an automatic toll tag, and motorcycles usually board first. The water is deep and dark, and in calm weather the mountains reflect in it so cleanly that you cannot tell where the cliff ends and the image begins. In wind, the surface turns steel grey and the air smells of salt and diesel.

For the road beyond, the surface is good, the traffic is light and the scenery changes quickly from sea level to high mountain. Roads here are narrow, with tunnels and sharp bends, and speed limits are strictly enforced with cameras and police. Weather matters, because fog and rain can arrive quickly, and temperatures drop sharply as you climb. In late autumn and winter, some of the mountain roads close because of snow, so check conditions in advance.

Fuel is a practical question. A fuel stop is listed here, but services in small places can be limited, with unmanned pumps that take cards only. Jørpeland, about fourteen kilometres away, is a town of more than five thousand people, and Hommersåk, Tau and the Stavanger area have more. Fill up if you have the chance, because the roads beyond the fjord are long and stations are far apart.

Food in these small places is simple, often a kiosk with waffles, hot dogs and coffee, or a small cafeteria in the ferry terminal. Norwegian waffles with brown cheese or jam are a decent lunch. If you can, bring a flask and a sandwich, and enjoy a quiet moment on deck.
t.lysebotn hairpins@59.1,6.7:
The Lysevegen, the road up from Lysebotn, is one of the engineering curiosities of Norway. It climbs about nine hundred metres from the head of the fjord to the plateau above in twenty-seven hairpin bends, which are numbered on small signs as you ride. The road was opened in the 1980s after a long struggle to link this remote village to the rest of the country, and it includes a tunnel in which the road itself makes a hairpin inside the rock. At the top, the plateau opens into a vast, bare landscape of rock and lakes, and the wind can be strong. A warm layer is wise even in summer, and the first view back down the hairpins is worth stopping for.
t.sirdal high road@58.9,6.8:
The Sirdal plateau is the high, open country behind the fjords of southwestern Norway, and it feels like another world. After the steep walls of the Lysefjord, the land flattens into a wide upland of bare granite, heather and small lakes, with the horizon open on every side. Few trees grow here, and the wind is a constant companion. Between the lakes stand scattered cabins, often painted red or left to weather grey, and in winter the whole area becomes a cross-country and downhill ski region.

The valley of Sirdalen cuts through the plateau, and its river, the Sira, has long been used for power. Tonstad, the nearest settlement of note at about twenty-three kilometres, is home to a large hydroelectric station that draws on the mountain reservoirs, and the area has been shaped by dams and tunnels. For centuries, though, the plateau was the domain of farmers who grazed sheep in summer and moved down in winter, and the sheep still wander freely across the open land.

The bends are long and open, the gradients are gentle, and the road runs across the plateau with wide views and little shelter. It is fast and flowing, but wind can be fierce, and the weather changes in minutes. Fog can come down and reduce visibility to a few metres, and rain can arrive sideways. Temperatures at nearly a thousand metres are often several degrees lower than at the coast, and even in summer a warm layer is worth wearing. Sheep, and occasionally reindeer on other plateaux, can stand on the road, so keep your speed sensible.

Services are limited. Tonstad has fuel and shops, but it is some distance away, and there are few stations on the plateau, so start with a full tank and carry a spare layer. Some mountain lodges and cafés open in the summer season, serving coffee, waffles and simple meals, but hours vary, so do not rely on them.

The light up here is wonderful, especially in late afternoon, when it picks out the ridges and the lakes. In autumn the heather turns red and bronze, and the air is clear and cool. It is a place to ride slowly and look.
t.byrkjedal food@58.8,6.3:
Byrkjedal is a small place in the hills of Gjesdal, inland from the Lysefjord and the Stavanger area, and it has the feel of a farming community on the edge of the high country. The name suggests birch valley, and the surrounding land is a mix of pasture, small lakes and birch woods, with low mountains rising to the east. The landscape here is shaped by ice, with rounded rocks, scattered boulders and thin soil, and the sheep and cattle graze on grass that grows fast in the brief summer.

This is not a tourist honeypot, and that is why the stop is welcome. After the crowded viewpoints of the fjord, a quiet roadside place feels honest. Norwegian rural food is simple and good, with coffee, waffles and sometimes a hot meal of meatballs or fish cakes, and it tends to be served with patience and a minimum of fuss. A slice of brown cheese on a waffle is a regional treat, sweet and slightly caramel in flavour, and it goes well with strong coffee on a cold day.

The roads around Byrkjedal are good riding. They run through hills and valleys with moderate bends, fine surfaces and long views, and traffic is light, mainly local farm vehicles and commuters. In summer the light lasts late into the evening, and a ride in the long golden hour is memorable. Weather can change quickly, with rain arriving off the sea and cooling the air, and in autumn and spring the roads can be damp or covered with fallen leaves. In winter, snow and ice make riding impractical for most.

Fuel is not available at Byrkjedal. Jørpeland, about thirty-one kilometres away, is the nearest town of any size, with several stations, and Vikeså and Tonstad are smaller alternatives. Because distances in this part of Norway are long, it is wise to fill up whenever you pass a station and not wait until the gauge is low. Many Norwegian pumps are automated and accept cards only, so keep a card with a chip and PIN handy.

If you linger, take a walk beside the lake or along a farm track and listen. The birdsong in early summer is rich, and the smell of birch and wet grass is strong. It is a gentle place, and a good one to rest before the last stretch of the ride.
t.apache trail overlook@33.6,-111.3:
The Apache Trail is the old name for State Route 88, a road that winds through the Superstition Mountains northeast of Phoenix, and it began as a construction track. Conditions vary, and washouts or fire damage have closed sections in recent years, so check the state transport department's updates before heading out.

The Superstition Mountains stand as a ragged skyline, and the legend of the Lost Dutchman's gold mine, which supposedly lies hidden in them, draws treasure hunters to this day. Fish Creek Hill, a short descent with a steep grade and hairpins, is the most dramatic part. Traffic is light, but vehicles are slow, and dust hangs in the air behind them. Late afternoon light turns the rock a deep red and gold, and in spring the desert blooms with wildflowers after a wet winter.

Apache Junction, about twenty-seven kilometres away, and Gold Canyon are the nearest towns, and Globe lies at the far end. Fill up and carry water, because summer temperatures here can reach well above forty degrees Celsius and the desert is unforgiving. Tortilla Flat has a small restaurant and general store, famous for its prickly pear ice cream, but opening hours vary.

Mobile reception is patchy, so tell someone your route. Take your time, stop at the overlooks, and enjoy the silence broken only by wind and the occasional raven.
t.roosevelt lake@33.7,-111.1:
Roosevelt Lake is Arizona's biggest reservoir and a startling sight in the middle of a desert. Services are limited. Tonto Basin, about twenty-three kilometres away, has small shops and basic supplies, and Globe, to the east, is the nearest place with a full range of services. There are marinas and campgrounds with small stores, but hours vary, so bring water and snacks, and fill the tank before you leave the main roads.

When you reach the shore, take a moment to look at the dam wall and the old stonework. It is a piece of history that still does its job.
t.globe@33.4,-110.8:
Globe is a copper town, and it wears that fact openly. Prices for fuel can be a bit higher than in Phoenix, but the convenience is worth it, and repairs are possible if something goes wrong.

The surrounding roads climb through pine and oak in the Pinal Mountains and lead eastward toward the San Carlos Apache lands. t.wunu mountain city@41.3,125.4:
Wunu Mountain City is a ruined fortress on a flat-topped crag in Liaoning province, in the green hills of northeastern China, and it was probably the first capital of the Goguryeo kingdom. Inside, there are traces of buildings, a spring, a soldier's quarters and a platform that may have served as a lookout. The air stays cooler up there and the views over the reservoir are some of the best in the region. Roads in this part of China are well surfaced, but tourist coaches and trucks make them busy at peak times, and the local style of overtaking takes getting used to.

Autumn is the time to come, when the oaks and maples turn yellow and red, and the sky is clear. Summer is warm and humid with heavy rain from July to August. Winters are deeply cold, with snow, and the stairway can be icy.

Huanren has fuel stations, a handful of simple restaurants and some local specialities. The area is known for ginseng and for freshwater fish from the reservoir, served stewed with tofu in iron pots, and for the strong flavours of northeastern Chinese cooking. Ji'an, a longer ride to the southeast on the Yalu River, holds the great tombs and the capital's later remains, including the huge General's Tomb, and is the obvious next stop for anyone following the story.

Visiting rules for foreign riders in China are strict, since driving requires a local licence and registration. Most visitors travel with a driver or guide.
t.aalborg@57.1,9.9:
Aalborg sits on the Limfjord, the broad, shallow waterway that cuts across northern Jutland and turns the northern tip of Denmark into an island, and the city has always been shaped by the water. It was a medieval trading town on the narrowest crossing, and today a bridge and a tunnel carry traffic over the fjord to Nørresundby on the north bank. The waterfront has been redeveloped with a promenade, a concert hall and the Utzon Center, designed by the architect of the Sydney Opera House, who had family roots in the area, and the old brick warehouses are full of cafes and bars.
