The land is mostly flat to gently rolling, with big fields, small woods and hedgerows, and the roads are well kept and speed limits strictly observed, with cameras in many places. The wind is a constant, and it can be strong off the fjord and the North Sea. Corners are mild, so the pleasure is in rhythm and sky rather than technical demands. Traffic is light outside the city, and the early morning light on the water is lovely.

With over a hundred thousand people in the city, there are stations everywhere, and all the services you could need. Danish prices are high, so a packed lunch can save money, though a hot dog from a roadside stand is a proper local treat. The smell of Aalborg is of salt water and the faint sweetness of the aquavit distillery. Plan your day around a long loop south toward Fyrkat and back along the fjord, and leave time for the burial ground at Lindholm Høje, where the sheep graze among the stones.
t.aalborg@57.0,9.9:
Aalborg is Denmark's fourth city, a university and industrial town of over a hundred and twenty thousand on the south bank of the Limfjord, the broad, shallow waterway that slices North Jutland nearly in two. The old harbour has been turned from shipyards and warehouses into a promenade, with the Utzon Center, designed by Jørn Utzon of Sydney Opera House fame, standing at the water's edge. Aalborg is also home to a well-known caraway-flavoured akvavit, which has been distilled here since the nineteenth century, and a May carnival that fills the streets with costumed students in what is often described as the largest in Northern Europe.

History goes deeper than the carnival. Across the fjord at Nørresundby, just over a kilometre away, the Lindholm Høje site holds a large Viking and Iron Age burial ground on a hillside, with graves marked by stones set in boat shapes. A short stop there gives you a much clearer picture of why this crossing mattered a thousand years ago. Today, the old ferry has been replaced by a bridge and a tunnel, and the traffic funnels through them on weekday mornings, so time your crossing.

Riding in North Jutland is gentle and wide, not dramatic. The land is low, rolling and farmed, with big skies, white churches, red-brick farmsteads and woodland that suddenly opens onto dunes. Roads are in excellent condition, and the bends are mild. Wind is the main character. A westerly off the North Sea can lean on you hard along the coast, and in autumn, rain squalls move through quickly. Speed cameras and police checks are routine here, and limits are taken seriously by locals, so keep to them. Summer is lovely with long evenings, when light lingers until nearly eleven.

Aalborg is easy for everything practical. There is fuel at many stations on the ring roads and on both sides of the fjord, plenty of cafes and bakeries in the centre, and ample parking near the harbour. The Marguerite Route, a signed tourist drive named for the white flower, passes through the area and links villages and coast. For a break, the harbour front is a pleasant place to sit with a pastry, watching the ferries and the grey-blue fjord.
t.christiansfeld@55.4,9.5:
Christiansfeld is a town that was planned on a drawing board by religious refugees, and it looks like it. In 1773 the Moravian Church, a Protestant brotherhood from Bohemia and Saxony, founded the settlement on land granted by the Danish king Christian VII, and laid it out with strict geometry: a central square, straight streets, identical yellow-brick houses with red-tile roofs, and a plain white church at the centre. UNESCO listed it as a World Heritage Site in 2015, and the unity of the architecture is startling, a whole town that feels like a single idea.

The most moving part is the graveyard, which the Moravians call God's Acre. Its stones are all the same, small and flat, set in orderly rows, because in death everyone was equal. Men and women lay in separate halves, and the plain grass and the lines of white markers make a quiet, beautiful place. Another tradition is more cheerful: Christiansfeld is famous for its honey cakes, thin, spiced biscuits baked here since the eighteenth century, and you can buy them in the old bakery.

For riders, the Danish roads are a different proposition from the German ones. The speed limits are low, the enforcement is strict, and the penalties are heavy, so you need to pay attention to every sign. Dipped headlights are expected at all times, and Danes drive politely and without hurry. The landscape of eastern Jutland is gently rolling, with farms, woods and low hills and fjords cut into the coast, and the roads wind sweetly through it, with good surfaces and little traffic outside the towns.

With about twenty-seven hundred people, Christiansfeld is small, but should have a filling station and a few cafés, and the larger town of Haderslev, twelve kilometres away, has plenty of everything. Danish prices are higher than in Germany, so a coffee and a pastry may sting, but the pastry will be worth it. Park in the square and walk the streets slowly, looking at the yellow brick in the light.
t.ranmou tomb and huanwen tomb@41.2,126.3:
It is a striking frontier: on one bank, Chinese towers and tourist boats; on the other, small farms, fishermen and a few watchtowers. The river is quiet, wide and slow here, and on a misty morning the contrast is haunting.

The tombs belong to Koguryo, the ancient kingdom that ruled much of Manchuria and the Korean peninsula from the first century BC until 668. Its second capital was here, and around Ji'an are hundreds of burial mounds, some of them stone pyramids, others earth-covered chambers with painted walls. The paintings show hunting scenes, dancers, guardians and the daily life of the elite, in colours that have survived for fifteen centuries. Ranmou and Huanwen are among the mural tombs that can be seen, and they are part of a UNESCO listing from 2004.

China does not generally allow foreign motorcyclists to ride their own bikes without elaborate permits and a guide, and the North Korean side is closed to independent travel, so most visitors come by train or car, or on an organised tour. If you do plan to travel here, check the rules carefully and arrange everything before you go. The region is cold in winter, with long frozen months, and warm and green in summer.

Fuel and services are in Manp'o on the far side and in Ji'an on this side, a city with hotels, restaurants and shops. The local food is Korean-Chinese, with cold noodles, dumplings and grilled meat. The best season is early autumn, with clear skies and the first colour in the hills. Take a warm layer in the evening, and look across the river, where the other country begins.
t.wandu mountain city@41.2,126.1:
Wandu is the mountain fortress that Koguryo's rulers built to retreat to when their lowland capital was threatened, and it still stands above the Yalu valley, a long line of stone walls following the contours of a steep ridge. Its builders chose a site where cliffs and slopes made natural defences, and the gates, towers, lookout platforms and palace foundations are visible in the forest. It is a place of long silences and big views, the sort of site that makes the strategy of the old kingdom obvious.

The city of Ji'an, a short distance below, was Koguryo's capital for about four centuries, until the court moved to Pyongyang in 427. The fortress was the backup: a place to hold when the plain was lost. Together with Guonei, the lowland city, and the tombs scattered in the valley, it makes up the UNESCO World Heritage listing of the Capital Cities and Tombs of the Ancient Koguryo Kingdom. The walls are made of carefully cut granite blocks, laid without mortar, and in places they stand several metres high.

The climb to the fortress is on foot, on a steep path through oak and pine forest. It takes some effort but is rewarded with views over the Yalu and across to the hills of North Korea. In autumn, the woods are gold and red, and in spring, wild azaleas bloom on the slopes. The weather is continental, with cold, dry winters and warm, humid summers, and mist often fills the valley in the mornings.

As for riding, this region requires planning. China does not generally allow foreign visitors to ride their own motorcycles without special permits and a guide, so check the rules before you set off. The nearest big town is Manp'o across the river, and on the Chinese side Ji'an has fuel, shops, hotels and restaurants. Try the local mountain vegetables and grilled fish, and drink plenty of water on the climb. A good pair of shoes matters more than anything on this site.
t.capital cities and tombs of the ancient:
Few places show the ambition of a lost kingdom as clearly as the valley of the Yalu at Ji'an, where Koguryo built three cities and left forty tombs that UNESCO listed in 2004. The kingdom began in the first century BC, grew into a regional power and fought off Chinese dynasties for centuries, and at its height it controlled territory from Manchuria to the middle of the Korean peninsula. Its warriors rode armoured horses, its builders cut huge blocks of granite, and its artists painted the walls of tombs with scenes that still glow.

The tombs are the most dramatic remains. The General's Tomb, a seven-tiered pyramid of granite blocks, stands on a hillside, and is often called the Pyramid of the East. It dates from the fifth century and is thought to be the burial place of King Gwanggaeto's son, or perhaps of the king himself. Nearby, a great stone stele, six metres tall, is inscribed with more than a thousand characters recording the king's conquests. The tomb murals, in the smaller chambers, show hunting, wrestling, music and mythical beasts in vibrant mineral colours.

The Yalu here is a border river, with North Korea on the far bank, and the valley is cold in winter and humid in summer. Mist in the mornings gives the hills a softness, and in autumn, the maples and birches turn yellow and red. There are signs of an old frontier everywhere: watchtowers, barbed wire, small ferries and fishermen.

A word of caution about the ride: China has strict rules about foreign motorcyclists, and you generally cannot just bring a bike across the border. Most visitors arrive by train or car or with a tour. Allow a full day to see the main sites, take water and sun protection, and bring a warm layer in the evening, when the temperature drops.
t.guonei city@41.1,126.2:
Guonei was the first capital of Koguryo on the Yalu, the city to which the court moved in the first years of the Common Era, and it grew into a significant centre. The name means something like the inner kingdom, and the city lay on a flat terrace by the river, protected by mountains on three sides. Its stone walls, built to enclose the palace, the markets and the houses, were several kilometres long, and traces of them can still be seen in the streets of modern Ji'an, which has been built over the old town.

Walking in Ji'an you find fragments of the past among the shops and apartment blocks. A section of the ancient wall stands between buildings, built of rough-cut stone, and a museum in the town holds finds from the tombs, including roof tiles stamped with faces, gilt-bronze ornaments, and pottery. The Gwanggaeto stele, a tall inscribed stone from the early fifth century, stands in its own pavilion, and, with its long text, it is one of the most important documents of early Korean history.

The setting is beautiful. The Yalu River curves past the town, wide and green, with Korea on the far bank, and fields of corn and rice spread over the plain. In the surrounding hills, the ridges rise in layers, and autumn colour makes them glow. The weather is harsh in winter, with temperatures below minus twenty, and pleasant in summer, with warm days and cool nights.

The ride here is more complicated than most. China restricts foreign motorcyclists, who normally need a temporary licence, a guide and a registered route, and independent riding is not generally possible. Most visitors come by train, by car or by organised tour. Manp'o, on the other bank, is part of North Korea and is not open to casual travel. If you are visiting Ji'an, you will find fuel, hotels, restaurants and a modest museum, and local dishes such as cold noodles and grilled river fish. Spend a half day in the town and another at the tombs, and take your time.
t.sedona@34.9,-111.8:
Sedona's red rocks look so unreal that visitors often assume they have been lit for effect. Cathedral Rock, Bell Rock, Courthouse Butte and a ring of cliffs the colour of rust and terracotta rise from the juniper and cypress woodland around the town, and in the early morning and at sunset, the light catches the sandstone and turns it fiery. The colour comes from iron oxide in the layers of rock, deposited over hundreds of millions of years, and then carved by wind and water into spires and buttes. About ten thousand people live in the town itself, at around 4,350 feet, in a place that has grown from a few orchards and a small post office in the early twentieth century, when it was named after Sedona Schnebly, the wife of an early settler.

It passes Bell Rock, Courthouse Butte and Cathedral Rock, with wide shoulders and pull-offs and a series of roundabouts, and the road is smooth and relaxed. Traffic is the main problem, since Sedona is one of the most visited places in Arizona, and weekends and holidays can mean long queues of cars. A Red Rock Pass or another recreation permit is needed for parking at many trailheads.

Oak Creek Canyon, to the north on US 89A, offers the better ride. The road drops into a deep canyon with steep walls, pine forest and a clear stream, in a series of tight switchbacks, with some of the sharpest corners found in Arizona. The air is cooler and the shade welcome in summer. Beyond the canyon, the road climbs to Flagstaff, past stands of aspen, and the contrast with the red rock below is striking.

Fuel and food are easy in Sedona, with plenty of cafes, bakeries and Mexican and southwestern restaurants. Rooms are expensive, so book ahead. Many visitors talk about vortexes, spots of supposed spiritual energy, and shops sell crystals and tours. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with warm days and cool nights, while July brings heat and thunderstorms.
t.oanes@58.9,6.1:
Oanes is a ferry quay on the Lysefjord, and for the Ryfylke route it is the traditional doorway. A short ferry crossing from Lauvvik brings you here, to the north shore of the fjord's mouth, and the road then heads east and north into the Ryfylke district, a landscape of fjords, waterfalls and steep mountain farms. There is not much at Oanes itself: a few houses, a bridge that carries the road over the water to Forsand, and a view back toward the cliffs. Hommersåk and Jørpeland, each over five thousand people, are the nearest places with real services, about thirteen kilometres away.

The ferry is part of the experience. The crossing takes about ten minutes, and in summer, the queue can be long, so arrive early and be prepared to wait. Once across, the road runs through Forsand, a village below the great wall of the Lysefjord's cliffs, and the stone-age and Viking settlement of Sandnes is nearby, with ancient rock carvings. Preikestolen, the famous cliff platform, is within reach on foot from a car park a short drive away, and the walk takes a couple of hours.

Ryfylke is one of the old lands of Norway, with a long history of farming, fishing and timber. The fjords here were used by Vikings, and burial mounds and standing stones mark the landscape. Today, the area is a mix of farms, fish farms and hydropower, and the roads are generally narrow, with many tunnels and bridges, built in the last few decades. The route is a National Tourist Route, with art installations and viewpoints along the way. The surface is good, and bends are frequent but not severe.

Weather is a gamble, and Rogaland is one of the wetter parts of Norway, with frequent rain and low cloud. In summer, though, there are days of sun, and the light on the fjord is beautiful. Fuel is available at Jørpeland and in the larger villages, but supplies in the more remote parts are limited, so keep an eye on the gauge. Cafes serve coffee, waffles and open sandwiches, and the small fish smokehouses sell trout and salmon. Take your time, and let the ferry settle your mind for the ride ahead.
t.roldal@59.8,6.8:
Røldal is a village high in the mountains of Vestland, near the border with Rogaland, and it sits in a bowl of peaks beside a lake. The landscape is the high fell, with snowfields on the surrounding mountains even in summer, and the road that leads in from either side climbs through tunnels, hairpins and open plateau. The village is small, with a population of a few hundred, and its main attraction is a stave church built in the thirteenth century, one of the oldest in Norway, which housed a miraculous crucifix that was said to sweat on Midsummer Eve. People came on pilgrimage in the Middle Ages, and the tradition continues. Odda and Sauda, about thirty kilometres away, are the nearest towns.

Røldal is a good place for a rest at the end of the Ryfylke route. The mountains around are popular for hiking and for winter sport, with a ski resort on the slopes above the village, and the lake, Røldalsvatnet, is calm and deep. Skiers go to the nearby Røldal Skisenter even in early summer, because snow often lasts into June. The pass above the village, the Haukelifjell, is one of the main routes between east and west Norway, and the road is kept open in winter as far as possible, though it can close in storms.

The riding is excellent. The road climbs through a series of bends and tunnels, with views of waterfalls, lakes and bare rock, and the gradient is moderate. The surface is generally very good, as this is a main road, and trucks and tourists share it in summer. Weather is the great variable: even in July, you can meet fog, rain and near-zero temperatures on the plateau, so carry warm layers. In autumn and winter, snow and ice are likely.

Fuel is available in Røldal, though prices are high, and there are cafes and a hotel. Local food includes waffles, cured meats and trout from the lake. The air is cold and clean, and in the evening, the light on the snow is a delight. After the long ride through Ryfylke, the village makes a good place to sit and watch the mountains turn blue.
t.bore@58.8,5.6:
Bore sits on the coast of Jæren, the flat, wind-brushed farmland south of Stavanger, and the landscape here is unlike the rest of Norway. There are no fjords or high mountains: the land is low and open, with fields of grass and potatoes, stone walls, and a long beach of pale sand backed by dunes. The farmers of Jæren are some of the most productive in the country, and the region is known for its dairy farms and vegetable fields. Bryne, about nine kilometres away, is a market town of around eight thousand, and Sandnes is the larger city, so fuel and supplies are not a problem.

The beaches are the draw. Bore, Hellestø and Orrestranda are long stretches of sand, popular with surfers, who ride the Atlantic swell in thick wetsuits all year round. The dunes are protected, and the wind is nearly constant, making the coast a place for kites and windsurfers. The surf scene is surprisingly lively, and cafes by the beaches serve coffee and waffles. On a warm day in summer, the sea may be inviting, though it is never warm.

The riding on the Jæren route is relaxed, with easy curves, flat terrain and wide views of the sea. The road follows the coast, passing through farmland and small villages, with an occasional glimpse of the North Sea. Wind is a major factor, and it can be strong enough to push the bike across the lane, so keep a firm grip. The surface is generally good, and traffic is light, apart from weekends in summer. In winter, storms can be fierce, and the road may be icy.

The area is rich in history. Standing stones and burial mounds from the Bronze Age and Viking Age dot the fields, and the Hå Gamle Prestegard, an old vicarage, has been turned into a cultural centre. Hå also has one of the best preserved lighthouses on the coast. Locals celebrate the cheese and the local waffles, and strawberries from the farms in June are a delight. The light on the flat land is clear and bright, and in the evening, the sunset over the North Sea lingers.
t.flekkefjord@58.3,6.7:
Flekkefjord is a town on the south coast of Norway, built around a narrow tidal inlet, and it is known as Little Holland, thanks to the old Dutch timber trade. In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, Dutch merchants bought timber here, and the old quarter, Hollenderbyen, is a district of white wooden houses with narrow lanes and small gardens, built by wealthy merchants and sea captains. The town has about five and a half thousand people, with a harbour, a bridge, a few shops and a pleasant waterfront. Fuel and supplies are easy, and Liknes and Moi are small towns nearby.

The town has a long maritime history, with shipping and shipbuilding, and the Flekkefjord Museum tells the story of the old trades. The fjord itself is narrow and sheltered, with steep sides and a deep green colour. The Dutch influence is visible in the architecture and in the street names, and the town is proud of its heritage. The surrounding area is a landscape of low, rounded hills, granite outcrops, forests and lakes, quite different from the fjords of the west coast.

The ride from Jæren is a quiet coastal route that follows the edge of Norway's southern tip, with a mix of farmland, forest and rocky shore. The road crosses a number of bridges and passes through tunnels, with views of islands and sea. The surface is generally good, the bends are gentle, and traffic is light. In summer, the weather is warm, and the south coast is one of the sunniest parts of Norway, so it is popular with Norwegian holidaymakers. Sudden rain showers are possible, and the wind off the sea can be cool.

Nearby, the Hunnedalen valley has an ancient route, and the Sirdal and Setesdal valleys lie to the north. The Jøssingfjord, further east along the coast near Egersund, was the setting for the Altmark incident of 1940, when the British navy boarded a German ship in the fjord to free British prisoners, an event that helped to drag Norway into the war. Food in Flekkefjord reflects the sea: shrimp, mackerel and fish soup are typical, and the cafes in the old town offer coffee and cake. A walk through the old quarter in the evening is a fine way to end the ride.
t.apache trail point 2@33.5,-111.4:
Canyon Lake is a surprise: a long, narrow reservoir of deep turquoise water, tucked among red cliffs and saguaro-covered slopes in the middle of the Sonoran Desert. It is one of a chain of lakes on the Salt River, created by dams built in the 1920s to supply water and power to the Phoenix area, and it has the look of a fjord in a desert. The road runs along its shore with a series of bends that give a view across the water to the dark cliffs of the Superstitions.

The lake is a popular spot for boating, kayaking and fishing, and a small marina near the road offers rentals. A tour boat called the Dolly Steamboat takes visitors on a trip along the lake, and gives the guide a chance to point out bighorn sheep, bald eagles and peregrine falcons on the cliffs. The desert here is full of life, with coyotes, javelinas, rabbits and roadrunners, and in the early morning you may see mule deer coming to the water.

For riders, this is the best stretch of the paved section. The road is narrow, winding and well surfaced, with sweeping turns, small climbs and dips, and views across the lake on one side and rock walls on the other. It is not a road for speed. There are blind corners, and the edges are rough in places, with little or no guardrail. Cyclists and tourists often wander across the lane, so keep to your side. Traffic can be heavy on winter weekends, and early morning is the quietest.

Fuel is not available here. The nearest stations are in Apache Junction, about seventeen kilometres back, so make sure you are full before you start. The marina has a small store with drinks and snacks, and a lakeside restaurant is open on some days, but hours vary. Restrooms are available at the picnic areas.

The cliffs here glow in the late afternoon, turning rich shades of red and orange, and the lake reflects them in a deep blue. In spring, wildflowers bloom along the road, including poppies and lupines after good winter rains. In summer, the heat is intense, and most visitors come in the cooler months.

A short stop at one of the pull-outs is rewarded with silence, broken only by the wind and the occasional bird call.
t.apache trail point 3@33.5,-111.4:
Tortilla Flat is a town that is mostly a saloon. The population is usually given as six, and the entire community consists of a restaurant, a general store, a gift shop and an ice cream parlour, all in old wooden buildings in a little valley between rocky hills. It began as a stagecoach stop on the road to Roosevelt Dam, and later served as a camp for construction workers, and it has been catering to travellers ever since.

The saloon is the star. Its walls and ceiling are covered with dollar bills, signed and stuck up by visitors over the decades, and the bar stools are real saddles. Cheerful staff serve burgers, chilli and cold beer, and the shop next door sells prickly pear ice cream, a pink and slightly floral scoop that tastes better than it sounds. Boardwalks connect the buildings, and a small desert garden of cacti stands behind. It is touristy, but in an honest, enjoyable way.

For the rider, Tortilla Flat marks a change. The paved road continues for a few miles, then the surface turns to graded gravel, and the character of the ride shifts from sightseeing to adventure. The dirt section, about twenty miles, is generally passable on a touring bike when dry, but it is narrow, steep and exposed, with washboard sections and loose gravel, and it can close after heavy rain. Ask at the shop about conditions before continuing, and consider whether your bike and tyres are up to it. Many riders turn around here and ride back, which is a perfectly good choice.

Drinks, snacks and meals are available, and the store sells water. The mobile signal is patchy, and a breakdown could mean a long wait, so ride with a partner if possible and carry basic repair tools.

The surrounding hills are the home of saguaro, ocotillo, cholla and palo verde, and in spring after wet winters the desert blazes with flowers. Mornings are cool and the light is soft, and by noon the heat is strong. The best way to enjoy the town is to arrive early, have a coffee on the porch, and let the cheerful silliness of the place settle in.
t.apache trail point 4@33.6,-111.3:
Fish Creek Hill is the part of the Apache Trail that people remember, and some wish they had not. The road, by this stage a graded dirt track, drops down the side of a canyon in a series of steep, narrow switchbacks, with a very steep grade, loose gravel and a sheer drop on the outer edge. There are no guardrails to speak of. The colours of the rock are extraordinary, with bands of red, orange, yellow and white, and from the overlook at the top you can see the canyon winding below.

The road was built to support Roosevelt Dam, which was begun in 1903. Workers carved the route out of the cliffs using dynamite and mules, and it was the only way to bring in cement, machinery and food. It was named after the Apache people who had used trails in the area, and today it is a National Scenic Byway, although it has the quality of a frontier track. It is also an area of fascinating geology, with ancient volcanic tuff, a rock made of compressed ash, which has been eroded into spires, ledges and shadowy gullies.

Riding the hill demands concentration and a bike that is up to it. The surface is rough, and the corners are tight, and a heavy touring bike will be a handful. Go slowly, use low gear and engine braking, and keep to the inside of the road. Oncoming traffic may include large vehicles, and you may have to reverse to find a passing place. The road is often closed after rain, and the surface can become slick or washed out. If in doubt, turn back. Several riders each year come to grief here, and rescue is far away.

Make sure your tank is full before leaving Tortilla Flat, and carry spare water. Mobile phone coverage is poor, and a satellite messenger is a worthwhile investment if you are riding alone.

The creek at the bottom of the hill runs in wet weather, and the canyon is cool and shaded. Look for hawks and ravens riding the thermals above, and for lizards on the warm rocks. In spring the canyon is green after winter rain, and the cactus flowers bloom.

Take your time, and use the pull-outs to look. The colours are best in the afternoon.
t.apache trail point 5@33.7,-111.2:
Theodore Roosevelt Dam is a stone fortress in a desert gorge, and when it was finished in 1911 it was the tallest masonry dam in the world. It holds back the Salt River to form Roosevelt Lake, a vast sheet of blue water in the dry hills of the Tonto Basin, and it was the first major project of the new US Reclamation Service, built to supply water to the farms and cities of the Phoenix valley. The dam was named for the president who had pushed through the Reclamation Act, and who came to dedicate it himself.

The original structure was built from huge blocks of local sandstone, cut and laid by hand, and the work took nearly eight years. In the 1990s it was enlarged and encased in concrete, raising its height, and some people regret that the old stone face is hidden. A modern bridge crosses the river just below the dam, with a view over the spillway and the lake, and a visitor centre tells the story.

The ride to this point is a hard-won one if you came by the dirt road, and the arrival has a certain satisfaction. The road leads past the lake, with views across the water to bare hills and cactus, and then along the old dam crest. The paved road continues east toward Globe and north to Payson, with good surface and gentle curves. Traffic is light, apart from fishing trucks and boats.

Services are modest. A few kilometres away, the small community of Roosevelt has a marina, a store and a basic cafe, and Tonto Basin, about twenty-two kilometres to the north-west, has fuel, a general store and a few restaurants. Plan fuel carefully, and fill up whenever you can. Camping is available at several sites along the lake, and a small lodge has rooms with views.

Not far away, the cliff dwellings of Tonto National Monument, built by the Salado people in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, sit in caves high above the lake. A short climb leads to the ruins, which have survived remarkably well because of the dry climate. The hike is steep, and the heat can be intense, so go early.

The lake is home to bald eagles in winter, and the hills turn green after rain. Spring is the best time for a ride, with flowers in bloom and mild weather.
t.norwegian scenic route ryfylke point 5@5:
Røldal is a village that most riders pass through without realising how much sits behind the petrol-station-and-bakery impression. It lies on the western rim of the Hardangervidda plateau, beside a long lake, with the road to Haukeli climbing steeply out of its eastern edge. Odda lies to the north-west, the larger town for any serious errands, and Sauda is the other neighbour in the opposite direction.

The stave church is the reason to stop. It is a small timber building of medieval origin, much altered over the centuries, and it holds a crucifix that has drawn pilgrims for hundreds of years. Tradition says the figure sweated or bled on Midsummer Eve, and the faithful once travelled across the mountains to be healed by it. Whatever you make of the legend, the interior has an intimacy that big cathedrals never manage, and the smell of old pine and tar is worth the five minutes.

The riding on either side is first class. Coming up from the west on the old road you get tight bends, retaining walls and a sense of the plateau looming above. Heading east, the E134 pushes up through snow-prone country toward the Haukelifjell. The pass is modern and well-engineered now, but it can still close in bad weather outside summer, so look at the traffic information before you commit in spring or autumn. Wind on the exposed sections can be fierce, and fog on the plateau can arrive in minutes.

Nature here is a mix of fjord-country lushness below and bare, wind-scoured plateau above, with reindeer and sheep on the higher ground and the lake mirroring the slopes on a calm morning. Photographers love the village in the low light of September.

As for supplies, Røldal is small, so if you need a full range of services treat Odda as the dependable town in the area. Pick a calm morning, give yourself a decent coffee, and let the church and the lake slow your day down before the mountain starts shouting.
t.lysevegen hairpins point 1@59.1,6.7:
Lysebotn lies at the bottom of the Lysefjord, one of the long, dark, steep-sided fjords of southwest Norway, and it is reached only by water or by a road so dramatic that it has become one of the most famous in the country. The village itself is tiny, a handful of houses, a quay and a campsite wedged between water and wall, and the mountain above it rises almost a kilometre straight up.

Most riders come for the road, the Lysevegen, which climbs out of the village in a series of twenty-seven hairpins. It was opened in the early 1980s and is a monument to patient engineering, with tight corners stacked one above another and a tunnel in which the road spirals inside the mountain. The surface is good, but the bends are steep and tight, so you need to be careful about gears and brakes, particularly on a loaded bike. Passing is tricky and coach traffic is common in summer.

The Lysefjord is about forty kilometres long, cut by glaciers into the granite, and the walls are so steep that sunlight reaches the village for only part of the day. The fjord is best known for Preikestolen, the flat cliff-top that draws walkers from across the world, and for Kjerag, the great boulder wedged in a crevice nearby, which has become a place of pilgrimage for BASE jumpers. A visit to Lysebotn gives you a good look at the head of the fjord from below.

The air here is cool and damp, and the smell of wet rock and conifer is strong. Waterfalls fall down the cliffs in rain, and the water in the fjord is deep and dark. The road is open in the summer season and closed in winter, usually from late autumn, so check dates before you come.

Services in the village are modest, and Jørpeland, a good thirty-five kilometres away by road, is the town for a full range of supplies. Go early in the morning if you can, when the light is soft and the traffic is light.
t.lysevegen hairpins point 2@59.1,6.7:
There is a moment on the Lysevegen, about halfway up, when the road disappears into the mountain and you realise someone decided that the best way to climb a cliff was to drill a spiral through it. That is the feel of this section, the upper part of the famous hairpins above Lysebotn, where the road swings back and forth up the face of the rock with the fjord opening out below you. The engineers did not so much conquer the mountain as persuade it.

The riding demands concentration. The hairpins are tight and steep, with a surface that is mostly good but often damp, and the combination of altitude, gradient and passing traffic means that smooth, deliberate throttle and clutch work counts more than speed. Use the engine to control the descent and give campervans room. The reward is the view, which opens out across the fjord and its tangle of cliffs and falls.

The road was built in the early 1980s, a late arrival in the history of Norwegian roads, to bring the isolated village at the fjord head into contact with the plateau above. Until then, Lysebotn was reached by boat, and its people lived by farming and fishing and the small trade of the fjord. A hydroelectric power station tucked into the mountain has long brought energy and employment to the district, and some of the engineering visible beside the road is a remnant of that.

The nature is sensational. Rock walls streaked with water, mountain birches clinging to ledges, and the fjord shining far below. Ravens and eagles ride the updrafts, and in the cool air there is a smell of wet stone and resin that is hard to forget. Mist and low cloud can fill the fjord, turning the drive into a trip through a dream.

There is no town on this stretch, and the nearest large settlement of any size is Jørpeland, some thirty-five kilometres away. Bring what you need and ride in daylight, in dry weather if you can choose. The road is closed in winter.
t.lysevegen hairpins point 3@59.0,6.7:
Come down into Lysebotn in the evening and you notice the silence first. The fjord is so enclosed that sound seems to be absorbed by the walls, and the only moving things are the water, the mist on the cliffs and the occasional boat nosing in to the quay. This is the bottom of the hairpins, the point where the long descent ends and the real shelter begins, and it is a very good place to stay for a night.

Lysebotn has the feel of a settlement that was never meant to exist. For centuries it was a handful of farms reached by boat, with grazing on narrow ledges and winters dark enough that the sun disappears behind the mountain for weeks. A hydroelectric station built into the rock brought power and work, and the road that came later made the place accessible by land. Passenger boats still arrive from the Stavanger side in summer, and many visitors come that way, taking in the fjord at water level.

For riders, the interest is in what comes next. Behind you lies a descent that is easier to enjoy when you are not tired, and ahead the mountain stands like a stack of stone shelves. If you plan the climb for the morning, you will have cool air, long shadows and few cars. If you arrive in the afternoon, the coach groups will be there before you.

Above the village the cliffs rise to the great plateau of Kjerag, where the famous wedged boulder draws walkers and parachutists alike. You do not have to climb it to appreciate the scale, but the sight of tiny figures on the rim is a good lesson in perspective. Wildlife includes peregrines and eagles, and sheep graze incongruously on impossibly steep grass.

Services are modest and there is no large town. Jørpeland is the nearest place with a full set of facilities, about thirty-five kilometres away by road. The route is closed in winter. Watch for wet leaves and gravel on the lower bends in autumn.
t.lysevegen hairpins point 4@59.0,6.9:
The top of the Lysevegen is not the sort of summit that announces itself with a sign and a car park, at least not to a rider who has just spent a quarter of an hour climbing hairpins. Instead the land levels out, the walls fall away, and you find yourself on an upland of bare granite, small lakes and heather, the Sirdal highlands, with the great fjord hidden somewhere behind you. It feels like arriving on a different continent.

The riding on the plateau is gentler. The road wanders over low ridges and past tarns, with long straights and easy curves, and the surface is generally decent. The weather is the main risk: fog, rain and wind can sweep across the open ground in minutes, and in spring or autumn there can be ice on the road. Sheep graze freely, and they have strong opinions about right of way.

This is old grazing country. For generations, farmers from the valleys took their animals to summer pastures on the high ground, living in simple huts and making cheese. The landscape bears traces of that history in stone walls, old paths and clearings, and there is a good chance you will see walkers on a marked trail. Further along, the plateau tilts toward the Sirdal valley and a different pattern of settlement.

Nature here is a mix of bog, rock and low scrub, with cotton grass in summer and a sharp, clean smell of peat and wet heather. Golden plovers call over the moor and the occasional eagle quarters the ridges. At the viewpoint above the fjord, where the cafe stands for the summer season, you can look back along the great trench of Lysefjord.

A seasonal cafe at the top serves coffee and simple food in summer, but this is not a place to rely on for anything more. Jørpeland, far below on the coast, is the nearest sizeable town. The road is only open in the warmer months, usually from late spring, so check conditions before you plan the day. Ride it in the morning, and take your time on the way down.
t.near odda@59.9,6.6:
South of Odda, in the narrow valley that leads toward Røldal, the road runs right past one of the most photographed waterfalls in Norway. Låtefossen falls in two great white streams that meet at the bottom and pass under an old stone bridge, so close to the road that spray can soak you as you stand at the railing. It is about 165 metres high, and in early summer, when the snow is melting, it thunders.

The valley here is steep and wooded, with the Hardanger mountains rising on both sides and waterfalls coming off the slopes in several places. The old road through the valley, with its stone bridge, dates from the nineteenth century, when the route from Odda to Haukeli and eastern Norway was improved, and Låtefossen has been an attraction for travellers ever since. There is a small kiosk and parking area beside the falls in summer.

Odda, a few kilometres north at the head of the Sørfjord, is an industrial town with an interesting story: it grew around smelting works in the early twentieth century, powered by hydroelectricity, and the old zinc and carbide plants were once among the biggest in Europe. Today the town is better known as the base for the hike to Trolltunga, the rock ledge that sticks out over the Ringedalsvatnet, which draws crowds from around the world. The old industrial buildings, now partly protected, give the town an atmosphere unlike the tidier villages of the fjord.

The riding on this stretch is a mix of valley road, tunnels and a few tight bends near the falls. Traffic can be heavy in summer, especially around Låtefossen, where cars stop and people wander onto the road. Ride carefully. The road south climbs to Røldal and over the Haukeli mountains, and north it follows the Sørfjord past orchards, which flower in May and give the Hardanger region its fame for apples and cider.

Odda has fuel, shops, cafes and accommodation, and it is the place to stock up before the climb south. The Sørfjord is a lovely ride north toward Kinsarvik and Utne, with fruit stands selling cherries in summer.
t.near bryne@58.8,5.6:
Jæren is the flattest piece of Norway's west coast, and on the shore near Bore it feels almost like another country. A long beach of pale sand runs south behind low dunes and marram grass, the North Sea rolls in on broad lines of surf, and inland the land is a patchwork of green fields divided by grey stone walls. There are no fjords here, no mountains close to the sea, just a wide sky and the constant presence of wind.

The landscape was shaped by ice. When the glaciers retreated at the end of the last ice age, they left behind a thick layer of gravel, sand and rounded boulders, and for centuries the farmers of Jæren cleared the stones from their fields by hand, piling them into the walls that crisscross the land today. It was a poor and hard place to farm, and the writer Arne Garborg, who grew up here, described the struggle in his books. Today, with modern methods, Jæren is one of the most productive farming areas in Norway, known for dairy, meat and vegetables.

The coast here is popular with surfers, who come for the waves that roll in from the North Sea, and Borestranden ranks among the best surf beaches in the country, along with the others that stretch south along the shore. There are also important nature reserves, protecting dunes, wetlands and bird habitats, and in spring and autumn the beaches and lakes are busy with migrating birds.

The riding is relaxed. The Jæren scenic route follows the coast on small roads between farms and dunes, with long straights, gentle curves and good surface. Traffic is moderate, heavier near Stavanger and Sandnes, and the wind is the main factor: it can blow hard and steadily off the sea, making riding tiring on the exposed sections. The light here is soft and changeable, and on a clear evening the sunsets over the sea are spectacular.

Bryne, about nine kilometres inland, is the main town of the area, with fuel, shops and cafes. Sola, to the north, has Stavanger's airport. There are small cafes and kiosks near some beaches in summer, but otherwise the coast is quiet. Bring a windproof jacket, even on a warm day.
t.near bryne@58.7,5.5:
Orre is little more than an old church, a lake and a beach, but on the Jæren coast that is plenty. The church, a medieval stone building, stands on a strip of land between the freshwater lake Orrevatnet and the dunes of Orrestranden, one of the longest beaches in Norway, and the setting is a lesson in how thin the line between land and sea can be here. Storms have shifted the dunes many times over the centuries, and the church has stood its ground.

Orrevatnet is the largest lake on Jæren and an important bird habitat, with ducks, geese, swans and waders, and in spring and autumn it is a gathering place for migrating birds. The dunes and the beach are protected as part of a larger nature reserve along the coast, which covers wetlands, grassland and shore. A modern visitor building near the beach, built for the scenic route, offers a place to shelter and learn about the area.

Jæren has a strong local identity. It is known for its farmers, its religious traditions and its distinctive dialect, and for the painters who came here in the nineteenth century, attracted by the light and the stark landscape. The stone walls, the old farmhouses and the round boulders left by the ice give the area a character that is very different from the rest of western Norway. Locally the food is hearty, with lamb, dairy and vegetables from the fields.

The riding on this part of the scenic route is easy, with small roads between fields, dunes and lakes, few corners and a good surface. You will have the road mostly to yourself, except for summer weekends when people from Stavanger come to the beaches. The wind is the constant companion, and it can make the ride tiring on the most exposed stretches. The best time is a calm evening in late spring or summer, when the low sun lights the dunes and the lake.

Bryne, about seven kilometres inland, is the nearest town, with fuel, shops and cafes, and Nærbø to the south is another option. Orre itself has the beach, the church and the lake, which is enough for a quiet break. Walk out onto the beach and listen to the surf, and look back at the church against the sky.
t.near vigrestad@58.5,5.7:
Kvassheim lighthouse stands on a low, stony point on the southern Jæren coast, a short white tower attached to a keeper's house, looking out over a sea that has wrecked more ships than anyone could count. This coast has no natural harbours and no shelter, just a long, flat shore of boulders and sand, and before the lights were built, ships driven onto it in storms had little chance. The lighthouse was taken out of service in the late twentieth century and is now a visitor centre and cafe for the protected coastal landscape around it.

The shore here is part of the Jærstrendene landscape area, a long protected strip of beaches, dunes, stony headlands and grassland, and it is full of traces of the past: burial mounds, old farm sites and boat houses, as well as the harbours built later for small fishing boats. The rounded stones are everywhere, left by the ice, and on the beaches they form great banks that rumble when the waves pull back.

The riding is relaxed and atmospheric. The road follows the coast through farmland, with long straights and a few curves, and the surface is good. Traffic is light. The wind is strong and steady, especially in autumn and winter, and conditions can flip within the hour. The light on this coast is soft and changeable, and the sunsets over the sea can be spectacular. In spring the fields are green and the birds are busy, and in autumn the colours of the grass and the sky are rich and moody.

A short way south lies Brusand, with a long beach and dunes, and beyond it Ogna, where the scenic route ends and the landscape changes from flat Jæren to the rocky hills of Dalane around Egersund. Inland, the villages of Vigrestad and Varhaug are small but have shops, and Nærbø, a little further, has the old Hå vicarage, now a gallery, near the shore.

For fuel and food, Vigrestad and Varhaug are the nearest options, and Egersund, about twenty kilometres south, is the nearest larger town. The cafe at the lighthouse is open in season. Stop, walk out to the point, and watch the waves rolling in.
t.hjelmelandsvagen@59.2,6.2:
Hjelmelandsvågen is a small village on the shore of the Jøsenfjord, in the heart of Ryfylke, the fjord and mountain district northeast of Stavanger. It is the main settlement of Hjelmeland municipality, with a harbour, a ferry quay, a church, a few shops and a cluster of houses on the slope above the water, and it is a quiet place where the main event of the day is often the arrival of the ferry across the fjord to Nesvik.

Ryfylke is a region of deep fjords, steep mountains, small farms on narrow ledges and old villages along the shore, and it has a long history of farming, fishing and fruit growing. Hjelmeland is known for its fruit, especially apples and plums, which grow on the sheltered slopes along the fjords, and in late summer the orchards are heavy with fruit. The area also has a rich tradition of boatbuilding and trade, with goods carried by boat to Stavanger and beyond.

The village is on the Ryfylke National Tourist Route, which follows the fjords and valleys from Oanes near Lysefjorden to Sauda, using ferries and roads. The modern route also passes through the Ryfast tunnels, opened in 2019, which link Stavanger to Ryfylke under the sea and include the longest and deepest undersea road tunnel in the world. From here, the route runs north along the fjords toward Sand and Sauda, and south toward Jørpeland and the famous cliff of Preikestolen, which rises over the Lysefjord.

The riding on this stretch is a mix of shoreline road and short climbs, with tight bends, narrow sections and fine views over the fjords and mountains. Traffic stays thin, except for summer weekends. The surface is generally good. The weather can change fast, and the fjords can be wet and misty, but on a clear day the light on the water is beautiful, and the evenings in summer are long and soft.

Hjelmelandsvågen has a shop and the basics of village life, and the ferry crossing is short and frequent; for a wider choice of everything, including fuel stations, Jørpeland is the safer bet. Jørpeland lies about twenty-five kilometres south. Take a break on the quay, look across the fjord, and watch the ferry coming in.
t.near sand@59.4,6.3:
The Sandsfjord is one of the quieter arms of the great Boknafjord system, a long strip of dark water between steep, wooded mountains, and the village of Sand sits near its head where the Suldalslågen river comes down from the hills. Around here Ryfylke loses its coastal softness. The slopes get higher, the farms cling to whatever flat ground the ice left behind, and waterfalls hang off the cliffs after rain, which in this part of Norway means most days.

The river is what made Sand known. The Suldalslågen is one of Norway's most celebrated salmon rivers, home to unusually large fish, and British gentlemen anglers rented fishing rights here in the nineteenth century, leaving behind lodges and a certain reputation. In Sand there is a salmon observatory built beside the river, with a viewing window into the water at the foot of a waterfall, where in summer you can watch the fish resting before they attempt the leap. Upstream, the river comes out of the long lake Suldalsvatnet, and the valley beyond leads toward the high mountains of Setesdal and Hardanger.

The riding around here is good fjord country riding. The road along the Sandsfjord runs close to the water, with short tunnels cut into the rock, a few tight bends around headlands and some nice flowing sections. North of Sand, the scenic route continues to Sauda, an old smelting town at the head of its own fjord, and beyond it the mountain road to Hellandsbygd and Røldal, with the impressive Svandalsfossen waterfall roaring right beside the road. The surface is generally good, and traffic is light most of the year. In early summer the waterfalls are at their best, and in autumn the birch on the slopes turns yellow against the dark rock.

Sand is a small place, with a shop, a cafe or two, a hotel and the basics, and there is a ferry across the fjord at Ropeid. Sauda, about twenty kilometres north, is the larger town, with fuel and more services. Ryfylke can be wet, so carry waterproofs and enjoy the waterfalls as the compensation, because they really are at their best in the rain.
t.medicine hat@50.0,-110.7:
Rudyard Kipling passed through Medicine Hat in 1907 and described it as having all hell for a basement, a reference to the huge reserves of natural gas beneath the town. The gas was so plentiful that the city kept its street lamps burning day and night for years because it was cheaper than paying someone to turn them off, and it still calls itself the Gas City. Today Medicine Hat is a busy prairie city of more than sixty thousand people in the valley of the South Saskatchewan River, surrounded by dry grassland and deep coulees.

The landscape here surprises people who expect flat prairie. The river has cut a wide valley into the plain, with steep, eroded bluffs and badlands-like coulees. The name is said to come from a Cree or Blackfoot legend involving a medicine man's headdress, though the details vary. The Saamis Tepee, a giant steel structure built for the 1988 Calgary Winter Olympics and now standing beside the Trans-Canada Highway, is said to be the world's tallest tepee and overlooks an archaeological site where Indigenous people camped and hunted bison for thousands of years.

Medicine Hat also has an industrial past in clay. The local clay deposits fed brick and pottery factories, and the old Medalta Potteries site, with its beehive kilns, is now a museum that tells the story of the workers and the crockery shipped across Canada.

For riders on the Cypress Hills loop, Medicine Hat is the obvious base. It has every service: fuel, motorcycle dealers, restaurants and hotels. Highway 41 heads south across the open plain to the Cypress Hills at Elkwater, a long ride with gentle curves, little traffic and huge skies. Wind is the main challenge here: the prairie can blow hard, especially in spring and autumn, and gusts can push a bike across the lane. Summers are hot and dry, often among the sunniest in Canada, with thunderstorms building in the late afternoon. Watch for pronghorn antelope in the grasslands and for deer near the river valleys at dusk. And carry water: the gaps between services on the plain can be long.

Lampeland is a small village in Flesberg, in the lower part of Numedal, the long valley that runs north-west from Kongsberg into the mountains of southern Norway. The river Numedalslågen flows through the valley, wide and calm in places, rushing over rapids in others, and the road follows it, with forested slopes rising on both sides and farms on the valley floor.

Numedal is known for its medieval stave churches, and Flesberg has one of them, a small, dark wooden church dating back to the Middle Ages, though much altered over the centuries. Further up the valley, the stave churches at Nore and Uvdal are among the most beautiful in Norway, with painted interiors and carved portals.

To the south, Kongsberg was founded in the seventeenth century after silver was found in the hills, and the silver mines were for a time among the largest in Europe. The mines at Saggrenda are open for tours, with a train taking you deep into the mountain. The town also has a fine Baroque church, one of the largest in Norway.

For riders, Rv40 through Numedal is a lovely road, with gentle curves along the river and views of the valley and the mountains. Traffic is light, especially outside the summer holidays. Speed limits are low and strictly enforced in Norway, and speed cameras are common. Kongsberg has the full range of fuel and food; up the valley, the villages have a few shops and stations, spaced further apart the higher you go. As a photo stop, the river and the valley, with the forested slopes beyond, are classic Norwegian scenery.
t.muravera@39.4,9.6:
Muravera lies in the south-east corner of Sardinia, on the flat, fertile plain where the Flumendosa river reaches the sea. After hours of mountain road, the change of scene is striking: the land opens out into orchards, mostly citrus, with irrigation channels and small farms between the town and the coast. With about 4,400 people, it has the shops, bars and fuel you would expect, and neighbours such as Villaputzu and San Vito are only a few kilometres away. The nearest larger town is Maracalagonis, a good half hour back toward Cagliari.

The road here is the SS125, the Orientale Sarda, which runs along the eastern side of the island from Cagliari up toward Olbia. In this section it is less about the bends and more about the contrast. Behind you are the granite mountains of the Sarrabus, with their scrubby slopes of cork oak and maquis, while ahead the coast has long sandy beaches and clear water. The ride in from the mountains is a fine one, with big, flowing curves, and the surface is usually good, though patchy in places and with farm traffic and slow vans that can interrupt the rhythm.

Sardinia is old in a way that is easy to forget on a bike. The island is dotted with nuraghi, stone towers built by a Bronze Age culture, and this region has its own traces of mining and agriculture that shaped small communities. The Flumendosa has been dammed upstream for water and power, which matters to the farmers here more than to any visitor. Local food leans on the land: citrus, olives, cheese, and sea produce from the coast, and the bakeries in town are a reliable stop.

Best seasons are spring and autumn, when the air is warm and the countryside is green or golden. In July and August the heat can be considerable and the coast crowded with holidaymakers, so riding early and stopping for a long lunch is the sensible approach. If you have time to spare, follow a side road down toward the shore and look at the lagoon-like mouth of the river, where birdlife tends to gather in the reeds.
